topics.title: Cash & Cash Equivalents
topics.reading:
What counts as a cash equivalent

Cash equivalents are highly liquid, short-term (generally one year or less), high-quality instruments whose price barely moves with interest rates. They are the right home for an emergency fund, money needed within a year or two, and the "dry powder" portion of a portfolio. Their main risks are not default or price swings but purchasing power (inflation) risk and reinvestment risk — when they mature, the investor must reinvest at whatever short-term rate then prevails.

Insured bank deposits and FDIC coverage

Checking, savings, money market deposit accounts (MMDAs) and bank CDs are bank deposits, not securities. The FDIC insures them up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category (individual, joint, certain retirement accounts, trust accounts, etc.). A married couple can therefore have far more than $250,000 insured at one bank by using different ownership categories. FDIC insurance does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds (including money market mutual funds) or annuities, even if bought at a bank.

Trap: A money market deposit account (bank product) is FDIC insured; a money market mutual fund is a security and is not. Money market funds try to keep a stable $1 NAV but are not guaranteed.

Certificates of deposit

A traditional bank CD is a time deposit: fixed rate, fixed term, FDIC insured, and generally non-negotiable — to get out early, the depositor pays an early-withdrawal penalty to the bank. Negotiable (jumbo) CDs are large-denomination CDs (traditionally $100,000 and up, commonly $1 million round lots) that can be sold to another investor in the secondary market before maturity. They are money market instruments, unsecured obligations of the issuing bank, and insured only up to the FDIC limit. Brokered CDs sold through broker-dealers can be sold in the secondary market too, so their price can fall below par if rates rise.

Money market instruments

InstrumentIssuerKey facts
Treasury billsU.S. TreasuryMaturities of one year or less (up to 52 weeks); issued at a discount, mature at par; the difference is interest. Backed by full faith and credit; interest exempt from state and local tax. The benchmark "risk-free" rate.
Commercial paperLarge corporations (and finance companies)Unsecured short-term promissory notes, maximum maturity 270 days (exempt from SEC registration). Usually issued at a discount in large denominations; buyers are institutions and money market funds.
Bankers' acceptances (BAs)Bank-guaranteed time draftsUsed to finance imports and exports. A bank "accepts" (guarantees) a company's draft, which then trades at a discount until it is paid at maturity.
Negotiable CDsBanksLarge, tradable CDs, as described above.
Repurchase agreements (repos)Dealers and banksSale of securities with an agreement to buy them back, often overnight. Effectively a short-term collateralized loan.

Money market instruments are debt with maturities of one year or less. They typically trade in very large denominations, so retail investors usually own them indirectly through a money market mutual fund.

Discount yield example

A 1-year T-bill with a $1,000 face value is bought for $960. The investor receives $1,000 at maturity; the $40 difference is interest. The return on money invested is $40 ÷ $960 ≈ 4.17%. There are no coupon payments, which is why T-bills are said to be "issued at a discount."

Suitability

  • Liquidity needs and short time horizons point to cash equivalents.
  • Holding too much cash over the long run exposes clients to inflation eroding real value.
  • Cash equivalents have almost no interest rate (market) risk because maturities are so short.
Exam tip: If a question asks which investment has the least default risk and the least interest rate risk, the answer is usually the Treasury bill. If it asks which has the greatest purchasing power risk, look for the cash equivalent or the fixed-rate long-term bond.
keyPoints: Cash equivalents: maturities of one year or less, highly liquid, minimal price risk; main risks are inflation (purchasing power) and reinvestment risk.
FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; it never covers securities, including money market mutual funds.
Traditional CDs are non-negotiable (early-withdrawal penalty); negotiable jumbo CDs ($100,000+) trade in the secondary market.
T-bills: one year or less, issued at a discount, full faith and credit, exempt from state and local tax.
Commercial paper: unsecured corporate debt, maximum 270 days, exempt from SEC registration.
Bankers' acceptances finance international trade (imports/exports) and are guaranteed by a bank.
Retail investors usually hold money market instruments through money market mutual funds.

topics.title: U.S. Government, Agency & Mortgage-Backed Securities
topics.reading:
Treasury securities

Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, so they are considered free of default risk. Their interest is taxable at the federal level but exempt from state and local income tax. They are highly liquid, but longer maturities still carry significant interest rate risk.

SecurityMaturityHow it pays
T-billsOne year or lessIssued at a discount, mature at par
T-notes2 to 10 yearsSemiannual interest
T-bondsLonger than 10 years (issued as 20- and 30-year)Semiannual interest
TIPS5, 10 and 30 yearsFixed coupon rate applied to an inflation-adjusted principal
STRIPSVariousZero-coupon; bought at a deep discount, mature at par

TIPS

Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities adjust their principal with the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The coupon rate is fixed, but because it is applied to a rising principal, the dollar amount of interest rises with inflation. At maturity, the holder receives the greater of the inflation-adjusted principal or the original par. TIPS usually carry a lower coupon rate than a regular Treasury of the same maturity because inflation protection is built in. The annual upward principal adjustment is taxable in the year it occurs even though it is not received until maturity ("phantom income"), which makes TIPS best suited to tax-advantaged accounts.

STRIPS (Treasury zero-coupon bonds)

STRIPS are created when dealers separate the interest and principal payments of Treasury notes and bonds into individual zero-coupon securities. Because there are no coupons, there is no reinvestment risk — the return is locked in if held to maturity. But zero-coupon bonds have the greatest price volatility (interest rate risk) of any bond of the same maturity. The annual accretion of the discount is taxable each year even though no cash is received, so they are also popular in IRAs and for funding a known future need such as college tuition.

Agency securities

  • GNMA (Ginnie Mae) — a government-owned corporation within HUD. GNMA pass-throughs are the only agency mortgage securities backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. Interest is taxable at federal, state and local levels. Minimum investment is $25,000.
  • FNMA (Fannie Mae) and FHLMC (Freddie Mac) — government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs), publicly held companies (under federal conservatorship since 2008). Their securities carry an implied, not explicit, government backing, so they yield slightly more than GNMAs. Interest is fully taxable.
Trap: "Agency" does not automatically mean "full faith and credit." Only GNMA among the mortgage agencies carries the explicit guarantee.

Mortgage-backed securities and prepayment risk

A mortgage pass-through passes homeowners' monthly payments of principal and interest through to investors (pools pay monthly, not semiannually). The key risk is timing:

  • Prepayment risk — when interest rates fall, homeowners refinance, principal comes back early, and the investor must reinvest at lower rates. Upside is capped.
  • Extension risk — when rates rise, prepayments slow and the investor is stuck longer in a below-market security.

Because the average life is uncertain, MBS are quoted on an assumed prepayment speed and usually yield more than Treasuries of similar average life.

CMOs

A collateralized mortgage obligation repackages mortgage cash flows into tranches with different expected maturities and prepayment treatment. Planned amortization class (PAC) tranches have the most predictable cash flows (lowest prepayment and extension risk) because companion (support) tranches absorb the variability; companion tranches therefore have the most risk and higher yields. A Z-tranche (accrual tranche) receives no cash until earlier tranches are retired, behaving like a zero-coupon bond. CMOs backed by agency pools are often rated AAA, but the rating addresses default, not prepayment risk. They are complex and generally not suitable for unsophisticated investors, and liquidity can be thin for some tranches.

Asset-backed securities (ABS)

ABS are backed by pools of non-mortgage receivables such as auto loans, credit card balances, student loans and equipment leases. Credit quality depends on the underlying pool and on credit enhancements (overcollateralization, senior/subordinate structures). Like MBS, they can have prepayment risk.

Exam tip: Falling rates = prepayment risk (MBS, callable bonds). Rising rates = extension risk and price decline. A question asking which investment has "no reinvestment risk" wants a zero-coupon bond.
keyPoints: Treasury interest: federally taxable, exempt from state and local tax; notes 2-10 years, bonds over 10 years (20- and 30-year).
TIPS adjust principal for CPI; fixed coupon rate on a rising principal; annual adjustment taxed as phantom income.
STRIPS/zero-coupon bonds: no reinvestment risk, greatest price volatility for a given maturity, taxable accretion each year.
GNMA is the only mortgage agency with full faith and credit backing; FNMA and FHLMC are GSEs with implied backing.
Agency mortgage securities are taxable at federal, state and local levels.
MBS pay monthly principal and interest; falling rates cause prepayment risk, rising rates cause extension risk.
CMO PAC tranches have the most predictable cash flows; companion tranches absorb prepayment variability and are riskiest.
ABS are backed by auto loans, credit cards, student loans and other receivables.

topics.title: Corporate, Municipal & Foreign Bonds
topics.reading:
Corporate bonds: secured vs unsecured

Corporate bonds are debt obligations; bondholders are creditors, not owners, and are paid before any stockholder. Security affects both safety and yield.

  • Secured bonds are backed by specific collateral: mortgage bonds (real property), equipment trust certificates (rolling stock such as airplanes and rail cars — common for transportation companies), and collateral trust bonds (securities the issuer owns, held by a trustee).
  • Debentures are unsecured — backed only by the issuer's general credit and promise to pay. Debenture holders rank with general creditors.
  • Subordinated debentures rank behind debentures and other general creditors. More risk means a higher yield.

Liquidation priority (bankruptcy): secured creditors (to the extent of their collateral) → unsecured creditors, including debenture holders → subordinated debt → preferred stock → common stock last.

Bonds are issued under a trust indenture (required under the Trust Indenture Act of 1939 for most public corporate issues), which names a trustee who protects bondholders and spells out covenants, call features and sinking fund provisions. Most corporate bonds pay interest semiannually and are fully taxable at federal, state and local levels.

Convertible bonds

A convertible bond may be exchanged for a fixed number of shares of the issuer's common stock. The conversion ratio = par value ÷ conversion price. Because investors get the upside of the stock, convertibles pay a lower coupon than comparable non-convertible bonds. Conversion dilutes existing shareholders. When the stock price rises well above the conversion price, the bond trades like the stock; when the stock falls, the bond's value is supported by its value as a straight bond (the "investment value"). Conversion math is covered in the preferred and equity topic.

Municipal bonds

General obligation (GO)Revenue bond
BackingFull faith, credit and taxing power of the issuerRevenue from the project financed (tolls, water fees, airport fees)
Typical projectsSchools, parks, police stations — non-revenue producingToll roads, bridges, airports, utilities, hospitals
ApprovalUsually requires voter approval; may be subject to debt limitsNo voter approval; analyzed with a feasibility study
Credit analysisTax base, debt per capita, economic health of the areaCoverage ratio, rate covenants, demand for the facility

A double-barreled bond is a revenue bond also backed by the issuer's taxing power. Industrial development revenue bonds (IDRs) are backed by a corporate lease payment, so credit quality depends on the corporation.

Municipal taxation

  • Interest on most municipal bonds is exempt from federal income tax.
  • It is generally also exempt from state tax for residents of the issuing state ("triple tax-free" if local tax also applies and is exempted). Out-of-state munis are usually taxable by the investor's home state.
  • Bonds issued by U.S. territories (Puerto Rico, Guam, U.S. Virgin Islands) are exempt from federal and all state income taxes.
  • Capital gains on munis are taxable. Interest on certain private activity bonds is a preference item for the alternative minimum tax (AMT).
  • Because of the tax break, munis carry lower nominal yields and are most attractive to investors in high tax brackets — and generally unsuitable for IRAs and other tax-deferred accounts.

Foreign bonds

  • Eurodollar bonds — U.S. dollar-denominated bonds issued and traded outside the United States (by foreign or U.S. issuers). Not registered with the SEC. A U.S. investor has no currency risk because payments are in dollars.
  • Yankee bonds — U.S. dollar-denominated bonds issued in the United States by foreign issuers and registered with the SEC.
  • Foreign-currency bonds — denominated in another currency; the U.S. investor faces currency (exchange-rate) risk. If the dollar strengthens, the foreign payments convert into fewer dollars.
  • Emerging-market sovereign debt adds political/sovereign risk and often lower liquidity.
Exam tip: "Dollar-denominated" means no currency risk for a U.S. investor. Yankee = foreign issuer, in the U.S., in dollars. Eurodollar = outside the U.S., in dollars.
Trap: Municipal bond interest is tax-exempt, but gains from selling a muni above its purchase price (or accreted basis) are taxable.
keyPoints: Secured bonds: mortgage bonds, equipment trust certificates, collateral trust bonds; debentures are unsecured; subordinated debentures rank lower.
Liquidation order: secured creditors, unsecured creditors/debentures, subordinated debt, preferred, common.
Convertible bonds pay lower coupons in exchange for the conversion feature; conversion ratio = par ÷ conversion price.
GO bonds are backed by taxing power and usually need voter approval; revenue bonds rely on project revenue and a feasibility study.
Muni interest is federally tax-exempt, usually state-exempt for in-state residents; territory bonds are exempt everywhere; capital gains are taxable.
Munis suit high-bracket investors and are generally unsuitable for IRAs and other tax-deferred accounts.
Eurodollar bonds: dollar-denominated, issued outside the U.S., not SEC registered; Yankee bonds: foreign issuer, U.S. dollars, SEC registered.
Foreign-currency bonds expose a U.S. investor to currency risk; a stronger dollar hurts.

topics.title: Fixed Income Characteristics & Valuation
topics.reading:
Price and yield move inversely

A bond's coupon is fixed, so when market interest rates rise, existing bonds fall in price until their yield matches the market; when rates fall, prices rise. A bond trading above par ($1,000) is at a premium; below par, at a discount.

The yield measures

  • Nominal yield (coupon rate) — annual interest ÷ par. Never changes.
  • Current yield = annual interest ÷ current market price.
  • Yield to maturity (YTM) — the total return if held to maturity, including the gain (discount) or loss (premium) back to par. It assumes coupons are reinvested at the YTM.
  • Yield to call (YTC) — the same idea, but assuming the bond is called at the first call date.

Example: A 6% bond ($60 per year) priced at $1,200 has a current yield of 60 ÷ 1,200 = 5.0%. Priced at $800, its current yield is 60 ÷ 800 = 7.5%.

The yield ordering

Bond priced atOrder (lowest to highest)
PremiumYTC < YTM < Current yield < Nominal
ParAll yields equal
DiscountNominal < Current yield < YTM < YTC

Logic: a premium buyer loses the premium at maturity, so YTM is below current yield; if called early, the loss is absorbed over fewer years, so YTC is lowest. A discount buyer gains back to par, so YTM is above current yield; if called early, the gain comes sooner, so YTC is highest. For premium bonds, the yield to worst is usually the YTC.

Exam tip: Draw a seesaw: write N – CY – YTM – YTC in a line. Premium = the line slopes down (N highest); discount = it slopes up (N lowest).

Call and put features

A call feature lets the issuer redeem bonds early — issuers call when rates fall, so investors face reinvestment risk and capped price appreciation. Investors demand a higher yield on callable bonds; call protection (a period when the bond cannot be called) is valuable. A put feature lets the investor sell the bond back to the issuer at par, protecting against rising rates, so puttable bonds offer a lower yield.

Duration

Duration measures a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes, expressed in years (the weighted-average time to receive the bond's cash flows). Approximate price change ≈ −duration × change in yield. A bond with duration 8 falls roughly 8% if rates rise 1%.

  • Longer maturity → higher duration.
  • Lower coupon → higher duration. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity.
  • Lower market yields → higher duration.

So the most price-volatile bond is a long-term, low-coupon (especially zero-coupon) bond. Investors expecting rates to fall want high duration; those expecting rates to rise want short duration.

Credit ratings and spreads

S&P / FitchMoody's
HighestAAAAaa
Lowest investment gradeBBB (BBB−)Baa (Baa3)
Speculative (high yield / "junk")BB and belowBa and below

The credit spread is the extra yield a lower-quality bond pays over a Treasury of the same maturity. Spreads widen when the economy weakens (investors flee to quality) and narrow when the economy is strong. A downgrade raises the bond's required yield, so its price falls.

Liquidity and taxation

Treasuries are the most liquid bonds; many municipal and corporate issues trade thinly, so selling small lots may mean a wide bid-ask spread. Tax treatment: corporate interest is fully taxable; Treasury interest is state-tax-exempt; muni interest is federally tax-exempt.

Tax-equivalent yield

To compare a tax-free muni with a taxable bond: Tax-equivalent yield = municipal yield ÷ (1 − marginal tax rate). Going the other way, the after-tax yield on a taxable bond = taxable yield × (1 − tax rate).

Example: An investor in the 35% bracket considers a 3.9% muni. TEY = 3.9% ÷ 0.65 = 6.0%. A corporate bond would have to yield more than 6.0% to be better. A 7% corporate after tax yields 7% × 0.65 = 4.55%, which beats the muni. The higher the bracket, the more attractive munis become.

Trap: Divide by (1 − tax rate), don't multiply by (1 + tax rate). For 3.9% at 35%, 3.9 × 1.35 = 5.27% is wrong; the right answer is 6.0%.
keyPoints: Bond prices and yields move inversely; premium = above par, discount = below par.
Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price.
Premium: nominal > current yield > YTM > YTC. Discount: nominal < current yield < YTM < YTC.
Call features benefit issuers (higher yield to investor); put features benefit investors (lower yield).
Duration rises with longer maturity and lower coupon; a zero's duration equals its maturity; price change ≈ −duration × yield change.
Investment grade = BBB/Baa or higher; BB/Ba and below is speculative (junk).
Credit spreads widen in weak economies and narrow in strong ones.
Tax-equivalent yield = muni yield ÷ (1 − tax rate).

topics.title: Equity Types: Common, ADRs & Preferred Stock
topics.reading:
Common stock

Common stock represents ownership. Common stockholders elect the board, receive dividends if and when declared, and have a residual claim on assets — they are paid last in liquidation but have unlimited upside. Their liability is limited to the amount invested. Over long periods, common stock has provided the best protection against inflation (purchasing power risk) of the major asset classes, at the cost of higher volatility.

  • Authorized shares — the maximum the charter permits.
  • Issued shares — shares ever sold.
  • Outstanding = issued − treasury stock. Treasury stock is stock the company bought back; it has no vote and receives no dividends.

American Depositary Receipts (ADRs)

An ADR is a negotiable receipt issued by a U.S. depositary bank representing shares of a foreign company held in custody abroad. ADRs let U.S. investors buy foreign companies in U.S. dollars on U.S. markets, with dividends converted to dollars and paid by the depositary bank. Holders generally have voting rights and may exchange ADRs for the underlying shares.

Trap: ADRs trade in dollars but still carry currency risk — the underlying shares and dividends are in the foreign currency, so a rising dollar lowers the ADR's value. Foreign taxes withheld on dividends may be claimed as a foreign tax credit.

Preferred stock

Preferred stock is equity with a stated dividend (percentage of par, often $100 or $25 par) and priority over common for dividends and in liquidation. It normally has no voting rights. Because the dividend is fixed, straight preferred behaves like a bond: its price moves inversely with interest rates, and it offers little inflation protection.

TypeFeatureEffect on dividend rate
CumulativeMissed dividends accumulate in arrears and must be paid before common receives anythingLower (safer)
Non-cumulative (straight)Missed dividends are lostHigher
ParticipatingMay receive extra dividends beyond the stated rate when profits allowLower
CallableIssuer may redeem at a set price, typically when rates fallHigher (compensates investor)
ConvertibleExchangeable into a fixed number of common sharesLower
Adjustable-rateDividend reset periodically to a benchmark ratePrice stays near par

Cumulative example: A 6%, $100 par cumulative preferred skips its dividends for two years. Before common holders get any dividend in year three, the company must pay $6 + $6 in arrears plus the current $6 = $18 per preferred share.

Corporations that own other companies' preferred (or common) stock may deduct a portion of dividends received (the dividends-received deduction), which is why straight preferred is popular with corporate investors.

Conversion math

Conversion ratio = par ÷ conversion price. A $1,000 bond convertible at $40 converts into 25 shares; a $100 preferred convertible at $20 converts into 5 shares.

Parity means the convertible and the stock it converts into are worth the same amount.

  • Parity price of the stock = market price of the convertible ÷ conversion ratio.
  • Parity price of the convertible = market price of the stock × conversion ratio.

Example: A $1,000 bond convertible at $50 (ratio 20) trades at $1,120. Parity stock price = 1,120 ÷ 20 = $56. If the stock trades at $58, converting is worth 20 × $58 = $1,160 — more than the bond's $1,120 price, so an arbitrage opportunity exists (buy the bond, convert, sell the stock). If the stock is at $52, the bond (worth 20 × 52 = $1,040 as stock) is trading at a premium to conversion value, and converting would be a mistake.

Exam tip: Always find the conversion ratio first (par ÷ conversion price), then multiply or divide. Conversion price is fixed at issue; the market price of the convertible is what changes.
keyPoints: Common stockholders vote, have limited liability and a residual claim; paid last in liquidation.
Outstanding shares = issued shares − treasury stock; treasury stock has no vote and no dividends.
ADRs: issued by U.S. banks, trade in dollars in the U.S., dividends paid in dollars — but currency risk remains.
Preferred has dividend and liquidation priority over common, usually no vote, and is interest-rate sensitive like a bond.
Cumulative preferred: arrears must be paid before common dividends; callable preferred pays a higher rate; convertible pays a lower rate.
Conversion ratio = par ÷ conversion price.
Parity stock price = convertible's market price ÷ conversion ratio.

topics.title: Equity Characteristics: Voting, Rights, Dividends & Restricted Stock
topics.reading:
Voting: statutory vs cumulative

Common stockholders vote on board elections, stock splits, mergers and other major changes. They do not vote on dividends (the board decides).

  • Statutory voting — one vote per share for each seat; votes cannot be combined. Owner of 100 shares with 4 seats up can cast up to 100 votes for each of 4 candidates.
  • Cumulative voting — total votes = shares × seats, and they may be distributed in any way, including all for one candidate. The same holder has 400 votes and may cast all 400 for one candidate. Cumulative voting benefits minority (small) shareholders.

Preemptive rights and rights offerings

A preemptive right lets existing shareholders maintain their proportionate ownership by buying new shares before they are offered to the public. Shareholders receive one right per share owned. Rights are short-term (typically 30 to 45 days) and allow purchase at a subscription price below the current market price, so they have value. A holder may exercise, sell the rights, or let them expire (the worst choice, since value is lost).

Warrants

A warrant is a long-term (often several years, sometimes perpetual) right to buy stock from the issuer at a fixed exercise price that is above the market price when the warrant is issued. Warrants are commonly attached to bonds or preferred stock as a "sweetener" so the issuer can pay a lower rate. They pay no dividends and carry no vote. When exercised, the company issues new shares (dilution).

RightsWarrants
LifeShort (weeks)Long (years)
Price at issuanceBelow marketAbove market
Typical originPreemptive rights offering to existing holdersSweetener attached to a new bond or preferred

Dividends

Cash dividends are declared by the board; stock dividends and splits increase the number of shares but not the total value or the investor's total basis (basis per share falls). Key dates, in order:

  1. Declaration date — board announces the dividend.
  2. Ex-dividend date — first day the stock trades without the dividend. The share price is reduced by roughly the dividend amount. Under the current T+1 regular-way settlement cycle, the ex-date is the same business day as the record date.
  3. Record date — shareholders on the company's books receive the dividend.
  4. Payable date — dividend is paid.

A buyer must purchase before the ex-date to receive the dividend. Qualified dividends (from U.S. corporations and qualifying foreign corporations, where the stock was held more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-date) are taxed at the long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, 20%). Non-qualified (ordinary) dividends are taxed at ordinary income rates.

Liquidation priority

In liquidation: secured creditors → unsecured creditors (including debenture holders, general creditors) → subordinated debt holders → preferred stockholders → common stockholders last.

Restricted and control stock — Rule 144

Restricted securities are acquired in unregistered, private transactions (e.g., a private placement). Control securities are held by affiliates — officers, directors, or holders of 10% or more of the voting stock — even if bought in the open market. Rule 144 provides a safe harbor to resell them publicly:

  • Holding period for restricted securities: 6 months if the issuer is an SEC reporting company; 1 year if not.
  • Volume limit for affiliates: in any 90-day period, the greater of 1% of outstanding shares or the average weekly trading volume over the prior four weeks.
  • Form 144 notice is required if an affiliate sells more than 5,000 shares or more than $50,000 worth in a 90-day period.

Employee stock options

Incentive stock options (ISOs)Non-qualified options (NSOs)
Who can receiveEmployees onlyEmployees, directors, consultants
Tax at grantNoneNone (usually)
Tax at exerciseNo regular income tax, but the spread is an AMT preference itemSpread (market price − exercise price) taxed as ordinary compensation income
Tax at saleEntire gain is long-term capital gain if shares are held 2 years from grant and 1 year from exerciseGain above FMV at exercise is capital gain (basis = FMV at exercise)
Exam tip: ISO = "incentive" = favorable capital gains treatment but watch AMT. NSO = ordinary income at exercise. Selling ISO shares too soon (a disqualifying disposition) converts the spread at exercise into ordinary income.
keyPoints: Statutory voting: shares per seat; cumulative voting: shares × seats, may be concentrated — benefits minority holders.
Preemptive rights: short-term, subscription price below market, let holders keep proportionate ownership.
Warrants: long-term, exercise price above market at issuance, often a sweetener attached to bonds or preferred.
Dividend dates in order: declaration, ex-dividend, record, payable; buy before the ex-date to get the dividend; with T+1, ex-date = record date.
Qualified dividends are taxed at 0/15/20% long-term capital gains rates if the holding period test is met.
Rule 144: 6-month holding period (reporting issuer) or 1 year (non-reporting); affiliate volume limit is greater of 1% of outstanding or 4-week average weekly volume per 90 days.
ISOs: no regular tax at exercise (AMT preference), LTCG if 2 years from grant/1 year from exercise; NSOs: ordinary income on the spread at exercise.

topics.title: Equity Valuation: Fundamental, Technical, DDM & DCF
topics.reading:
Two schools of analysis

Fundamental analysis asks what to buy by estimating a company's intrinsic value. It studies the economy, the industry, and the company's financial statements, management, competitive position and earnings prospects. Tools include the balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement, and ratios such as P/E, price-to-book, return on equity, current ratio and debt-to-equity. If intrinsic value exceeds market price, the stock is considered undervalued.

Technical analysis asks when to buy by studying market data — price and volume patterns, not company fundamentals. Tools include:

  • Charts and patterns — trendlines, head-and-shoulders (a top pattern signals a reversal from bullish to bearish; an inverted one signals a bottom), consolidation.
  • Support and resistance — support is a price floor where buying emerges; resistance is a ceiling where selling emerges. A breakout through resistance is bullish; a break below support is bearish.
  • Moving averages — smooth price trends; price moving above its moving average is considered bullish.
  • Market breadth — the advance/decline line measures how many stocks rise versus fall.
  • Contrarian indicators — the odd-lot theory (small investors are assumed to be wrong) and short interest: a high short interest is considered bullish because short sellers must eventually buy to cover.
Trap: An analyst reading a balance sheet or looking at the P/E ratio is doing fundamental analysis. An analyst looking at trading volume, moving averages or short interest is doing technical analysis — even if the data concern one company.

Dividend discount model (DDM)

The DDM values a stock as the present value of its expected future dividends.

  • Zero-growth (a perpetuity): Value = D ÷ r. Also used for straight preferred stock. A preferred paying $5 per year with a required return of 8% is worth 5 ÷ 0.08 = $62.50.
  • Constant growth (Gordon growth model): Value = D1 ÷ (r − g), where D1 is next year's dividend, r is the required rate of return, and g is the constant dividend growth rate. The model requires r greater than g.

Example: A stock just paid a $2.00 dividend (D0). Dividends grow 5% a year and investors require 9%. First find D1 = 2.00 × 1.05 = $2.10. Value = 2.10 ÷ (0.09 − 0.05) = 2.10 ÷ 0.04 = $52.50. If the stock trades at $45, it appears undervalued.

The model shows that value rises when expected growth rises or when the required return falls (for example, when interest rates fall). It works best for mature, stable dividend payers and does not work for companies that pay no dividends.

Exam tip: Watch for "just paid" (D0) versus "expected next year" (D1). If given D0, grow it one year first. And rearranging gives the expected return: r = (D1 ÷ price) + g — dividend yield plus growth.

Discounted cash flow (DCF)

DCF analysis values any asset as the sum of the present values of its expected future cash flows, discounted at a rate that reflects risk (the required return or cost of capital). Present value of one future amount = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n.

Example: An investment will pay $1,100 in one year. At a 10% discount rate, PV = 1,100 ÷ 1.10 = $1,000.

  • Net present value (NPV) = PV of future cash flows − cost today. A positive NPV means the investment earns more than the required return; accept it. A negative NPV means reject.
  • Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes NPV = 0. For a bond, the YTM is its IRR.
  • A higher discount rate lowers present value; a lower discount rate raises it.

When a stock's DCF-derived intrinsic value is above its market price, a fundamental analyst views it as undervalued (a buy); below market price, overvalued.

Other valuation ratios

  • P/E ratio = market price ÷ earnings per share. Growth stocks typically carry high P/Es; value stocks low P/Es.
  • Dividend yield = annual dividend ÷ market price.
  • Price-to-book = market price ÷ book value per share; value investors favor low price-to-book.
keyPoints: Fundamental analysis (what to buy) studies financial statements, industry and economy to estimate intrinsic value.
Technical analysis (when to buy) studies price, volume, charts, support/resistance, moving averages and market breadth.
High short interest is a bullish (contrarian) technical indicator; odd-lot theory is also contrarian.
Zero-growth DDM: value = D ÷ r (also used for preferred stock).
Gordon growth model: value = D1 ÷ (r − g); if given D0, compute D1 = D0 × (1 + g).
DCF: value = sum of PVs of future cash flows; positive NPV means accept; IRR sets NPV to zero.
Intrinsic value above market price = undervalued.

topics.title: Equity Public Offerings: IPOs, Secondaries & SPACs
topics.reading:
Primary vs secondary distributions

In a primary offering, the issuing company sells new shares and receives the proceeds. In a secondary distribution, existing holders (founders, venture capital funds, affiliates) sell shares they already own, and the proceeds go to those sellers, not the company. Primary offerings increase shares outstanding (dilution); pure secondary distributions do not.

  • Initial public offering (IPO) — a company's first sale of stock to the public. The company then becomes a public, reporting company.
  • Follow-on (subsequent primary) offering — an already-public company sells additional new shares.
  • Combined offering — both new company shares and existing holders' shares are sold at once.

The registration process

Under the Securities Act of 1933, a non-exempt public offering requires a registration statement filed with the SEC. After filing, a cooling-off period of at least 20 days begins. During it:

  • No sales may be made and no binding orders accepted; indications of interest may be taken.
  • A preliminary prospectus ("red herring") may be distributed. It lacks the final offering price.
  • The underwriter conducts due diligence.

On the effective date, sales may begin and the final prospectus must be delivered. SEC effectiveness does not mean the SEC approved the security or vouched for the accuracy of the prospectus — claiming otherwise is illegal. Underwriters distribute the issue on a firm commitment (underwriter buys the whole issue and bears the risk) or best efforts basis (underwriter acts as agent; unsold shares return to the issuer).

A shelf registration lets eligible public companies register securities now and sell them over time (up to three years) as market conditions allow.

IPO risks and suitability

IPOs have no trading history, often high volatility, and frequently a limited public float. Company insiders usually agree to a lock-up period (commonly 180 days) during which they cannot sell; the expiration of lock-ups can pressure the price. Hot IPOs are often allocated primarily to institutional clients. For a retail client, an IPO is a speculative holding.

SPACs and blind pools

A special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) is a "blank check" shell company that goes public through an IPO with no operating business, intending to acquire a private company within a set period (commonly 18 to 24 months). Key features:

  • IPO proceeds are placed in a trust account (typically invested in Treasuries) until a deal is completed.
  • SPAC IPO units commonly include a share and a fraction of a warrant.
  • When a target is announced, shareholders can typically redeem their shares for a pro rata share of the trust instead of participating.
  • If no acquisition is completed by the deadline, the SPAC liquidates and returns trust funds to shareholders.
  • The merger with the target is called the de-SPAC transaction; it is a way for a private company to become public without a traditional IPO.
  • Risks: sponsors receive a large "promote" (founder shares) for little cost, creating conflicts of interest; dilution from warrants and sponsor shares; the target is unknown at the time of investment.

A blind pool is an offering in which the specific assets or businesses to be acquired are not identified at the time investors commit money (common in some real estate programs and direct participation programs). Investors rely entirely on the sponsor's judgment. A blank check offering is similar: a development-stage company with no specific business plan other than to merge with an unidentified company. Blank check offerings of penny stocks are subject to SEC Rule 419, which requires proceeds to be held in escrow until an acquisition is completed and approved by investors.

Trap: A SPAC investor does not know the target company when buying in the IPO — that is what "blank check" means. The trust account protects the IPO money, not the post-merger stock price.
Exam tip: Proceeds of a primary offering go to the issuer; proceeds of a secondary distribution go to the selling shareholders. Only primary offerings dilute existing holders.
keyPoints: Primary offering: new shares, proceeds to the issuer, dilutive. Secondary distribution: existing holders sell, proceeds to them, no dilution.
IPO = first public offering; follow-on = later primary offering by an already-public company.
Cooling-off period is at least 20 days; only a preliminary prospectus (red herring) and indications of interest, no sales.
SEC does not approve securities or guarantee prospectus accuracy.
Firm commitment: underwriter bears risk; best efforts: underwriter acts as agent.
SPAC: blank check company; IPO proceeds held in trust; shareholders can redeem; liquidates if no deal by deadline (often 18-24 months).
Blind pool: assets/businesses not identified when investors commit money.

topics.title: Pooled Investment Types: Mutual Funds, Closed-End Funds, UITs, FACs and ETFs
topics.reading:
Under the Investment Company Act of 1940, an investment company pools money from many investors and invests it in securities. The Act sorts investment companies into three types: face-amount certificate companies, unit investment trusts (UITs), and management companies. Management companies are further split into open-end (mutual funds) and closed-end funds. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are usually organized as open-end companies or UITs but trade like stocks.

Open-end management companies (mutual funds)

  • Continuous primary offering: the fund issues new shares whenever investors buy, so capitalization is not fixed. Because it is always in distribution, a prospectus must be delivered.
  • Redeemable: shareholders sell shares back to the fund at the next computed net asset value (NAV), less any redemption fee or contingent deferred sales charge. Payment must be made within 7 calendar days.
  • Only one class of security (common shares) is sold to the public; mutual funds may borrow from banks but may not issue senior securities such as bonds or preferred stock to the public.
  • Professional management, diversification, low minimums, automatic reinvestment, and exchange privileges within a fund family.

Closed-end management companies

  • A one-time IPO creates a fixed number of shares; after that the shares trade on an exchange or OTC.
  • Price is set by supply and demand and can be at a premium or discount to NAV. Investors pay a commission (or markup) rather than a sales load.
  • Not redeemable. May issue common stock, preferred stock and bonds, so closed-end funds often use leverage, which magnifies both gains and losses and makes income more volatile.
  • Because the manager never faces redemptions, closed-end funds can hold less liquid securities (e.g., municipal bonds, emerging-market debt).

Unit investment trusts (UITs)

A UIT buys a fixed portfolio of securities and holds it until a stated termination date. There is no board of directors and no investment adviser — the portfolio is supervised, not actively managed. Units are redeemable with the trust (the sponsor may also maintain a secondary market). UITs are common for fixed pools of municipal bonds and for some older ETFs. A UIT is an investment company, but not a management company.

Face-amount certificate companies

The investor pays a lump sum or periodic installments; the issuer promises to pay a stated face amount at maturity (or a surrender value if redeemed early). It is essentially a debt obligation of the issuer, which bears the investment risk. These are rare today, but the exam may ask you to identify them as one of the three types of investment companies.

Exchange-traded funds (ETFs)

  • Trade intraday on an exchange at market prices; investors can use limit orders, stop orders, short sales and margin — none of which are possible with a traditional mutual fund.
  • Market price stays close to NAV because authorized participants create and redeem large blocks ("creation units") in kind with the fund. Retail investors buy and sell in the secondary market, not with the fund.
  • Most ETFs are passively managed, so expense ratios are typically low. The in-kind redemption process makes ETFs generally more tax-efficient than comparable mutual funds (fewer capital gains distributions).
  • Costs to consider: brokerage commissions (often zero today) and the bid-ask spread, which makes frequent small purchases in thinly traded ETFs less efficient.
FeatureOpen-end fundClosed-end fundETFUIT
Shares outstandingUnlimitedFixed after IPOVaries via creation/redemptionFixed units
Where bought/soldFrom/to the fundSecondary marketSecondary marketSponsor/trust
PriceNAV (+ load)Market (premium/discount)Market, near NAVNAV-based
ManagementActive or passiveActiveMostly passiveNone (fixed portfolio)
Exam tip: "Trades at a premium or discount to NAV" and "fixed number of shares" point to a closed-end fund. "Redeemable" and "continuously offered" point to an open-end fund. "No board of directors and no investment adviser" points to a UIT.
Trap: Retail investors do not buy ETF shares from, or redeem them with, the fund, and ETFs do not use forward pricing. Mutual fund orders are always filled at the next computed NAV — you cannot place a limit order on a mutual fund.
keyPoints: Three types of investment companies: face-amount certificate companies, UITs and management companies (open-end and closed-end).

Closed-end funds have a fixed number of shares after the IPO, trade on exchanges at a premium or discount to NAV, and may use leverage.
UITs hold a fixed, unmanaged portfolio, have no board of directors or investment adviser, and terminate on a set date.
ETFs trade intraday at market prices and can be bought on margin, sold short and traded with limit or stop orders.
ETFs usually have low expense ratios and are tax-efficient because of in-kind creation and redemption, but investors pay the bid-ask spread.

topics.title: Private Funds (Hedge, PE, VC) and REITs
topics.reading:
Private funds

Hedge funds, private equity (PE) funds and venture capital (VC) funds are private funds: pools that avoid registering as investment companies by relying on an exclusion in the Investment Company Act and that sell their interests in private placements (typically under Regulation D) rather than public offerings. Because they are not registered, they provide much less disclosure, face few limits on leverage or concentration, and sell only to wealthy or sophisticated investors.

  • Section 3(c)(1) funds: limited to 100 beneficial owners; investors are generally accredited investors.
  • Section 3(c)(7) funds: no numerical cap in the Act, but every investor must be a qualified purchaser — for an individual, generally someone who owns at least $5 million in investments.

Accredited investor (natural person) basics under Regulation D:

  • Net worth over $1 million, alone or with a spouse or spousal equivalent, excluding the value of the primary residence; or
  • Income over $200,000 (or $300,000 joint) in each of the two most recent years with a reasonable expectation of the same this year; or
  • Holding certain professional credentials in good standing, including the Series 7, Series 65 or Series 82.

Hedge funds

Hedge funds use flexible strategies: short selling, leverage, derivatives, arbitrage, global macro bets. Despite the name, many are not "hedged" and can be highly risky. Typical features: a "2 and 20" style fee (a management fee on assets plus a performance fee on profits), lock-up periods during which money cannot be withdrawn, limited redemption windows (e.g., quarterly with advance notice), and limited transparency. Funds of hedge funds offer diversification across managers but add a second layer of fees.

Private equity and venture capital

PE funds buy controlling stakes in established private companies (often through leveraged buyouts) or take public companies private, improve them and exit through a sale or IPO. VC funds invest in early-stage, high-growth start-ups where most investments fail and a few large winners drive returns. Both are generally structured as limited partnerships, with capital commitments drawn down over time and fund lives of roughly 10 years — extremely illiquid and suitable only for a small portion of a wealthy investor's portfolio.

Real estate investment trusts (REITs)

A REIT is a company that owns (equity REIT) or finances (mortgage REIT) income-producing real estate; hybrid REITs do both. REITs let small investors own diversified real estate with professional management.

  • Tax treatment: if a REIT distributes at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders (and meets asset and income tests — roughly 75% of assets and income tied to real estate), it avoids corporate-level tax on the distributed income. This is conduit or pass-through treatment for income.
  • Losses do NOT pass through to REIT shareholders — a key difference from real estate limited partnerships.
  • REIT dividends are generally not qualified dividends, so they are largely taxed at ordinary income rates.
  • REITs are not investment companies; investors own shares of a corporation or trust.
Listed (publicly traded) REITNon-traded REIT
LiquidityTrades daily on an exchangeIlliquid; limited share-redemption programs that can be suspended
PricingMarket price, visible and volatilePeriodic estimated value; less apparent volatility
CostsCommission/spreadOften high up-front fees and offering costs
RegistrationSEC-registered and exchange-listedOften SEC-registered but not listed
Exam tip: REIT = 90% of taxable income distributed, pass-through of income only, dividends taxed largely as ordinary income. A client seeking real estate exposure with daily liquidity should use a listed REIT or REIT fund, not a non-traded REIT or a real estate limited partnership.
Trap: Do not confuse the 90% REIT distribution requirement with the 90% requirement for a regulated investment company (mutual fund) — both use 90%, but only REITs have real estate asset tests. And remember: a REIT never passes losses through.
keyPoints: Private funds (hedge, PE, VC) avoid investment company registration and sell via private placements to accredited investors or qualified purchasers.
Accredited individual: net worth over $1 million excluding primary residence, or income over $200,000 ($300,000 joint) in each of the past two years, or a Series 7, 65 or 82 license.
Qualified purchaser (individual): generally at least $5 million in investments; 3(c)(1) funds are capped at 100 beneficial owners.
Hedge funds feature leverage, short selling, performance fees and lock-ups; PE and VC are long-term, highly illiquid commitments.
REITs must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to avoid corporate tax on it; income passes through, losses do not.
REIT dividends are generally non-qualified and taxed largely as ordinary income.
Listed REITs trade daily; non-traded REITs are illiquid with high fees and limited redemptions.

topics.title: Fund Share Classes, Sales Charges, Pricing, Expenses and Taxation
topics.reading:
Pricing: NAV, POP and forward pricing

NAV per share = (total assets − total liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding. The public offering price (POP) is what a buyer pays: POP = NAV + sales charge. For no-load funds, POP = NAV. Mutual funds use forward pricing: orders are filled at the next NAV calculated after the order is received (generally at the 4:00 p.m. ET market close), never at a prior price.

The sales charge percentage is calculated on the POP, not on NAV: Sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP. Example: NAV $9.40, POP $10.00 → $0.60 ÷ $10.00 = 6.0%. To find POP from NAV: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %). With NAV $9.40 and a 6% load, POP = $9.40 ÷ 0.94 = $10.00. FINRA caps mutual fund sales charges at 8.5% of POP.

Share classes

ClassSales charge12b-1 feeBest for
AFront-end load deducted from the investment; breakpoints reduce itLow (often 0.25%)Large purchases and long holding periods
BNo front-end load; contingent deferred sales charge (CDSC) that declines each year (e.g., 5% down to 0% over about 6 years)Higher (up to 1%)Rarely suitable today; usually converts to A shares after the CDSC period
C"Level load": no front-end load, small CDSC (often 1%) for about the first yearHigher (up to 1%) for as long as heldShorter holding periods (a few years)

A 12b-1 fee is an annual asset-based fee used for distribution/marketing and shareholder services; it is included in the expense ratio. Under FINRA rules it cannot exceed 1% (0.75% distribution + 0.25% service), and a fund may call itself "no-load" only if its 12b-1 fee is 0.25% or less and it has no front-end or deferred sales charge.

Breakpoints, letters of intent and rights of accumulation

  • Breakpoints: reduced Class A sales charges at higher dollar levels (e.g., 5.75% under $25,000; 4.5% at $25,000; 3.5% at $50,000). Purchases may generally be aggregated for the investor, spouse and minor children, and across funds in the same family.
  • Letter of intent (LOI): the investor states an intent to invest enough within 13 months to reach a breakpoint and gets the reduced charge right away. The LOI may be backdated up to 90 days to cover a recent purchase. Shares are held in escrow; if the investor falls short, the higher charge is collected. Market appreciation does not count toward the LOI — only new money.
  • Rights of accumulation (ROA): when existing holdings in the fund family (valued at current value, or at cost if the fund's policy allows) plus a new purchase cross a breakpoint, the new purchase gets the lower charge. There is no time limit, but ROA does not reduce charges already paid on past purchases.
  • Breakpoint selling — recommending a purchase just below a breakpoint, or splitting purchases among fund families so the client misses a discount — is an unethical practice.

Expense ratio

Expense ratio = annual operating expenses ÷ average net assets. The biggest component is usually the management (advisory) fee; 12b-1 fees and administrative costs are also included. Sales loads and brokerage commissions on portfolio trades are not in the expense ratio. Index funds and ETFs usually have the lowest ratios.

Taxation of funds and shareholders

A mutual fund that qualifies as a regulated investment company under Subchapter M by distributing at least 90% of its net investment income pays no tax on what it distributes — the conduit (pass-through) theory. Shareholders are taxed on:

  • Dividend distributions (from interest and dividends): ordinary income, or qualified dividend rates to the extent the fund received qualified dividends.
  • Capital gains distributions: always long-term, regardless of how long the shareholder has owned the fund.
  • Distributions are taxable in the year paid even if reinvested; reinvested amounts increase cost basis.
  • Selling or redeeming shares creates a capital gain or loss that is short- or long-term depending on the investor's own holding period. Exchanges within a family are taxable sales.

Buying shortly before a distribution ("buying the dividend") hurts the client: NAV drops by the distribution and the client owes tax on what is effectively a return of their own money.

Benchmarks

Compare a fund with an appropriate index: S&P 500 (large-cap U.S.), Russell 2000 (small-cap U.S.), MSCI EAFE (developed international markets outside North America), Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index (investment-grade U.S. bonds), and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (30 price-weighted large-cap stocks).

Exam tip: Long holding period + large amount → Class A. Short holding period (1-3 years) → Class C. The sales charge percentage is always figured on POP.
Trap: Capital gains distributions are long-term even if the investor bought the fund last month. The investor's holding period matters only when the investor sells shares.
keyPoints: POP = NAV + sales charge; sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP; POP = NAV ÷ (1 − load %).
Forward pricing: mutual fund orders fill at the next computed NAV after receipt.
Class A: front-end load and breakpoints; Class B: declining CDSC and higher 12b-1; Class C: level load, best for short holding periods.
12b-1 fees max 1% annually; a fund can be called no-load only if its 12b-1 fee is 0.25% or less.
Letter of intent: 13 months to reach the breakpoint, may be backdated 90 days, shares held in escrow.
Rights of accumulation count existing family holdings toward breakpoints on new purchases; breakpoint selling is prohibited.
Funds distributing at least 90% of net investment income pass taxation to shareholders; capital gains distributions are always long-term and taxable even if reinvested.
Expense ratio includes management and 12b-1 fees but not sales loads or portfolio brokerage costs.

topics.title: Derivative Types: Options, Warrants, Rights, Futures and Forwards
topics.reading:
A derivative derives its value from an underlying asset — a stock, index, commodity, currency or interest rate. The exam expects you to recognize each type, know who holds which right or obligation, and know how each is traded.

Options

An option is a contract giving the buyer (holder, long) a right and the seller (writer, short) an obligation. The buyer pays a premium; the writer receives it. A standard equity option covers 100 shares, so a $3 premium costs $300.

Buyer (long) has the right to…Seller (short) has the obligation to…Market view
CallBUY the stock at the strike priceSELL at the strike if assignedLong call: bullish. Short call: bearish/neutral
PutSELL the stock at the strike priceBUY at the strike if assignedLong put: bearish. Short put: bullish/neutral

Memory aid: buyers of calls and sellers of puts are bullish; buyers of puts and sellers of calls are bearish.

  • In the money: a call when market price > strike; a put when market price < strike. Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount. Premium = intrinsic value + time value.
  • American-style options can be exercised any time up to expiration; European-style only at expiration.
  • Listed options are standardized and guaranteed by the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC), which virtually eliminates counterparty risk. Investors must receive the Options Disclosure Document before their account is approved for options.
  • Buyers risk only the premium; uncovered (naked) writers can face large or unlimited losses and must post margin.

Warrants and rights

Rights (subscription rights)Warrants
Issued byThe company, to existing shareholdersThe company, often attached to bonds or preferred stock as a "sweetener"
PurposeHonor preemptive rights — let holders keep proportionate ownershipMake the other security more attractive (allowing a lower coupon or dividend)
LifeShort-term (typically 30-45 days)Long-term (years; some perpetual)
Exercise priceBelow current market priceAbove market price when issued

Both are issued by the company, both are dilutive when exercised, neither pays dividends or carries voting rights, and both can be sold or allowed to expire. Holders of rights who do not want to buy more shares should sell the rights rather than let them lapse.

Futures

A futures contract is a binding obligation for both parties — the long must buy and the short must deliver — a specified quantity and quality of an asset at a set price on a future date. Futures are standardized, traded on regulated exchanges and guaranteed by a clearinghouse. Positions are marked to market daily and require margin (a performance deposit), so small price moves create large percentage gains or losses (leverage). Most contracts are closed out before delivery. Producers (farmers, miners) typically sell futures to hedge; users (food processors, airlines) buy futures to lock in costs. Futures are regulated by the CFTC.

Forwards

A forward is a private, customized agreement between two parties to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date — common in currencies and commodities among businesses and banks. Because forwards trade over the counter with no clearinghouse, they carry significant counterparty (default) risk and liquidity risk (they are hard to exit before maturity). Settlement generally occurs only at maturity; there is no daily mark-to-market.

FuturesForwards
TermsStandardizedCustomized
Where tradedExchangeOver the counter
Counterparty riskMinimal (clearinghouse)Significant
SettlementMarked to market dailyAt maturity
Exam tip: Options = a right for the buyer and an obligation for the seller. Futures and forwards = obligations for both sides.
Trap: Warrants and rights are issued by the company, so exercising them raises capital for the issuer and dilutes existing shareholders. Listed options are created by investors and cleared by the OCC — exercising a listed call does not create new shares.

Long calls and short puts are bullish; long puts and short calls are bearish.
Listed options are guaranteed by the OCC; American-style can be exercised any time, European-style only at expiration.
Rights: short-term, exercise price below market, issued to existing holders under preemptive rights.
Warrants: long-term, exercise price above market at issuance, often attached to bonds or preferred as a sweetener.

topics.title: Option Math and Hedging: Max Gain, Max Loss, Breakeven
topics.reading:
The Series 65 tests basic option positions, not complex spreads. Work every problem per share first, then multiply by 100 for one contract.

The four basic positions

PositionBreakevenMaximum gainMaximum loss
Long callStrike + premiumUnlimitedPremium paid
Short (naked) callStrike + premiumPremium receivedUnlimited
Long putStrike − premiumStrike − premium (stock falls to zero)Premium paid
Short putStrike − premiumPremium receivedStrike − premium

Memory aid: "Call up, put down" — for calls add the premium to the strike; for puts subtract it. The buyer and the seller of the same option share the same breakeven, and one side's maximum gain is the other side's maximum loss.

Example — long call: Buy 1 XYZ Jan 50 call at $4. Breakeven = $54. Max loss = $4 × 100 = $400. If XYZ rises to $61 and the call is closed at intrinsic value ($11), profit = ($61 − $54) × 100 = $700.

Example — long put: Buy 1 ABC 40 put at $3. Breakeven = $37. Max loss = $300. Max gain = ($40 − $3) × 100 = $3,700 if ABC goes to zero. If ABC is at $32 at expiration, profit = ($37 − $32) × 100 = $500.

Hedging with options

Protective put (long stock + long put) — insurance for a long stock position. The investor keeps unlimited upside (less the premium) and sets a floor at the strike price.

  • Breakeven = stock cost + put premium
  • Max loss = (stock cost − strike) + premium
  • Max gain = unlimited

Example: Buy 100 shares at $60 and buy 1 60 put at $2. Breakeven = $62. Max loss = ($60 − $60) + $2 = $2 per share = $200. Same stock with a 55 put at $1: max loss = ($60 − $55) + $1 = $6 × 100 = $600.

Covered call (long stock + short call) — generates income and gives a small cushion on the downside, but caps the upside. Best for a neutral to slightly bullish outlook.

  • Breakeven = stock cost − call premium
  • Max gain = (strike − stock cost) + premium
  • Max loss = stock cost − premium (stock goes to zero)

Example: Own 100 shares bought at $48; sell 1 50 call at $3. Breakeven = $45. Max gain = ($50 − $48) + $3 = $5 × 100 = $500. Max loss = ($48 − $3) × 100 = $4,500.

Short stock hedges: a short seller faces unlimited risk if the stock rises; buying a call caps that loss. Writing a put against a short position provides only partial protection equal to the premium.

Choosing the right hedge

Client holdsFearMaximum protectionIncome / partial protection
Long stockPrice declineBuy a putSell a call (covered call)
Short stockPrice riseBuy a callSell a put
Diversified portfolioMarket declineBuy index putsSell index calls

Costs, benefits and risks

  • Benefits: leverage (control 100 shares for a small premium), defined risk for buyers, hedging, and income generation for writers.
  • Costs: premiums and commissions; time decay erodes the value of long options as expiration nears.
  • Risks: buyers can lose 100% of the premium in a short time; naked call writers face unlimited loss; naked put writers can be forced to buy stock far above market; covered call writers give up upside above the strike.
Exam tip: Among the four basic option positions, only the uncovered short call has unlimited maximum loss. (A short stock position also has unlimited risk.)
Trap: In a covered call, the premium lowers the breakeven (cost − premium). In a protective put, the premium raises the breakeven (cost + premium). Don't mix up the direction.
keyPoints: Call breakeven = strike + premium; put breakeven = strike − premium (same for buyer and seller).

Long put: max gain = strike − premium; short put: max loss = strike − premium.

topics.title: Alternatives: Limited Partnerships, ETNs, Leveraged/Inverse Funds, Structured Products
topics.reading:
Direct participation programs and limited partnerships

A limited partnership (LP) is the classic direct participation program (DPP): income, gains, losses, deductions and credits flow through directly to the partners, who report them on a Schedule K-1. The partnership itself pays no federal income tax. Common programs include real estate, oil and gas, and equipment leasing.

  • General partner (GP): manages the business, has a fiduciary duty to the LPs, and has unlimited liability.
  • Limited partners: passive investors with liability limited to their investment (plus any recourse debt they are responsible for). If a limited partner takes part in management, limited liability can be lost.
  • Passive activity rules: losses from a passive activity can offset only passive income — not wages or portfolio income (interest, dividends, capital gains). Unused passive losses are carried forward and can be fully used when the investor disposes of the entire interest.
  • Illiquidity: there is usually no secondary market; transfers often need GP consent. LPs suit investors with long horizons, high income in need of tax benefits, and money they will not need.
  • Investors should evaluate the economic soundness of the program first — tax benefits alone never justify an investment. Publicly traded partnerships (MLPs) are the liquid exception, trading on exchanges.

Exchange-traded notes (ETNs)

An ETN is an unsecured, senior debt obligation of the issuing financial institution whose return is linked to an index or strategy. The ETN owns no underlying assets. Key points:

  • Credit (default) risk of the issuer: if the bank fails, investors are unsecured creditors — even if the index performed well.
  • No tracking error in the ETF sense, because the issuer promises the index return minus fees.
  • Typically pay no periodic interest; trade on an exchange; may be called by the issuer or suffer from limited liquidity; the market price can diverge from indicative value if the issuer stops issuing new notes.

Contrast: an ETF owns a portfolio of assets held separately in the fund — investors are not exposed to the sponsor's credit.

Leveraged and inverse funds

Leveraged ETFs seek a multiple (2x, 3x) of an index's return; inverse ETFs seek the opposite (−1x); leveraged inverse seek −2x or −3x. They use swaps, futures and other derivatives and reset daily — they target the multiple for one day only. Over longer periods, compounding causes returns to differ, often dramatically, from the multiple of the index's return, especially in volatile markets.

Example: An index starts at 100, rises 10% to 110, then falls 10% to 99 (−1% over two days). A 2x fund starting at $100 rises 20% to $120, then falls 20% to $96 (−4%, not −2%).

FINRA has warned that these products are generally unsuitable for retail investors who plan to hold them longer than one trading session, particularly in volatile markets. They are tools for sophisticated, actively monitored, short-term trading or hedging. They also typically carry higher expense ratios.

Structured products

Structured products (structured notes, market-linked CDs, principal-protected notes, reverse convertibles) combine a debt instrument with a derivative to deliver a payoff linked to an index, basket or stock. Common features:

  • Participation rate (share of the index gain credited), caps on upside, and sometimes partial or full principal protection at maturity.
  • Principal protection is only as good as the issuer's credit; it generally applies only if held to maturity.
  • Limited liquidity (often no active secondary market), complex payoffs, embedded costs that are hard to see, possible call features, and potentially complicated tax treatment.
  • A reverse convertible pays a high coupon but may repay the investor in depreciated stock if the reference stock falls below a barrier — the investor has effectively sold a put.
Exam tip: The one risk to name for an ETN (and for principal-protected notes) is the credit risk of the issuer. The one fact to know about leveraged/inverse ETFs is the daily reset, which makes them unsuitable for buy-and-hold.
Trap: Passive losses from an LP cannot offset a client's salary or dividend income. And an inverse ETF is not the same as a short sale — its loss is limited to the investment, but it still decays over time in volatile markets.
keyPoints: Limited partnerships pass income, losses, deductions and credits through to partners via Schedule K-1.
General partners manage and have unlimited liability; limited partners are passive with liability limited to their investment.
Passive losses offset only passive income; unused losses carry forward and are released when the entire interest is sold.
LPs are illiquid; judge economic soundness before tax benefits.
ETNs are unsecured debt of the issuer — the key risk is issuer credit risk; they own no underlying assets.
Leveraged and inverse funds reset daily; compounding makes them unsuitable for long-term holding by most retail investors.
Structured products combine debt with derivatives; principal protection depends on the issuer's creditworthiness and holding to maturity.

topics.title: Annuities: Fixed, Variable, Equity-Indexed and Their Taxation
topics.reading:
An annuity is a contract with an insurance company designed to accumulate money on a tax-deferred basis and then provide income, often for life. The purchaser is the owner; payments are based on the life of the annuitant; a beneficiary receives any death benefit.

Types

Fixed annuityVariable annuityEquity-indexed (fixed indexed) annuity
Who bears investment riskInsurerContract ownerMostly insurer (floor), owner shares upside
Where assets are heldInsurer's general accountSeparate account with subaccountsGeneral account
Security?No — insurance productYes — requires securities and insurance licenses and a prospectusGenerally not treated as a security
ReturnGuaranteed rateVaries with subaccountsIndex-linked with participation rate, cap and minimum guarantee
Key riskPurchasing power (inflation) riskMarket riskCaps limit upside; complex; surrender charges

The separate account of a variable annuity is registered as an investment company (typically a UIT or open-end fund). Variable annuities charge a mortality and expense (M&E) risk fee, administrative fees, subaccount expenses, optional rider fees and, usually, surrender charges for early withdrawals. Most offer a death benefit during accumulation that guarantees beneficiaries at least the amount invested (less withdrawals).

Accumulation units and annuity units

  • During the accumulation phase, payments buy accumulation units, whose value changes with the subaccounts (like mutual fund shares).
  • At annuitization, accumulation units are converted to a fixed number of annuity units. Each payment = number of annuity units × current annuity unit value, so payments vary.
  • The insurer sets an assumed interest rate (AIR). If actual subaccount returns exceed the AIR, the next payment rises; if returns equal the AIR, payment is unchanged; if returns fall short, payment falls — even if returns were positive.

Payout options (highest to lowest monthly payment)

  1. Life only (straight life): payments for the annuitant's life; nothing to heirs. Highest payment, greatest risk to the family.
  2. Life with period certain (e.g., 10 years): if the annuitant dies early, a beneficiary receives payments for the rest of the period.
  3. Unit refund life: beneficiaries receive any undistributed value.
  4. Joint and last survivor: payments continue until the second of two annuitants dies; typically lowest payment.

Taxation of non-qualified annuities

  • Contributions are made with after-tax dollars (they create cost basis); there are no IRS contribution limits. Earnings grow tax-deferred.
  • Withdrawals (not annuitized) are taxed LIFO: earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income; basis comes out last, tax-free.
  • A 10% penalty applies to the taxable portion withdrawn before age 59½, with exceptions for death, disability and annuitized (substantially equal) payments.
  • Annuitized payments use an exclusion ratio: part of each payment is a tax-free return of basis, the rest is ordinary income.
  • Gains are never capital gains, and there is no step-up in basis at death; beneficiaries owe ordinary income tax on the gain.

Example: Ana, 52, invested $80,000 in a non-qualified variable annuity now worth $130,000 and withdraws $60,000. Under LIFO the first $50,000 is earnings: taxable as ordinary income plus a 10% penalty ($5,000). The remaining $10,000 is return of basis, not taxed.

1035 exchanges

Section 1035 permits a tax-free exchange of: annuity → annuity, life insurance → life insurance, life insurance → annuity, and endowment → annuity. An annuity cannot be exchanged tax-free for a life insurance policy. The exchange must go directly between insurers. Switching can trigger a new surrender period and higher costs, so the recommendation must be in the client's interest.

Exam tip: Variable annuities are generally unsuitable for young investors with short horizons, for money needed before 59½, or inside an IRA purely for tax deferral (the IRA already defers taxes).
Trap: Payments go down when the separate account earns less than the AIR — even a positive 3% return lowers the payment if the AIR is 4%.
keyPoints: Fixed annuity: insurer bears investment risk, not a security; variable annuity: owner bears risk, is a security held in a separate account.
Equity-indexed annuities credit index-linked returns subject to participation rates and caps, with a minimum guarantee.
Accumulation units during accumulation; converted to a fixed number of annuity units at annuitization.
Actual return above the AIR raises the payment; below the AIR lowers it.
Life only pays the most per month; joint and last survivor typically pays the least.
Non-qualified withdrawals are LIFO: earnings first, taxed as ordinary income, plus 10% penalty before 59½.
No step-up in basis at death; annuitized payments use an exclusion ratio.
1035 exchanges: annuity to annuity, life to life, life to annuity — never annuity to life.

topics.title: Life Insurance: Term, Whole, Universal, Variable and Variable Universal
topics.reading:
Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured dies. The main purpose is to replace income or cover obligations (mortgage, education, estate taxes). Permanent policies also build cash value that grows tax-deferred.

Term insurance

Term insurance provides pure protection for a set period (e.g., 10, 20 or 30 years) and builds no cash value. It provides the most death benefit per premium dollar, so it is ideal for young families with large needs and limited budgets. Level term keeps the death benefit constant; decreasing term shrinks it (e.g., to match a mortgage). Premiums rise at renewal. Many policies are convertible to permanent coverage without new evidence of insurability.

Whole life

  • Fixed level premium, guaranteed death benefit and guaranteed cash value growth.
  • Cash value is invested in the insurer's general account; the insurer bears the investment risk. Participating policies may pay dividends (treated as a return of premium).
  • Owners can borrow against cash value; unpaid loans reduce the death benefit.

Universal life (UL)

  • Flexible premiums and an adjustable death benefit, within limits.
  • Cash value earns a current interest rate declared by the insurer, with a minimum guaranteed rate. Not a security.
  • If premiums are too low and cash value is exhausted, the policy can lapse.

Variable life (VLI)

  • Fixed premium; cash value is invested in a separate account of subaccounts chosen by the owner.
  • Cash value is not guaranteed and can fall. The death benefit has a guaranteed minimum (the initial face amount) and can rise with good performance.
  • A security: requires a prospectus and both securities and insurance licenses.

Variable universal life (VUL)

  • Combines UL's flexible premiums and death benefit with VLI's separate account investing.
  • Neither cash value nor death benefit is guaranteed beyond what is maintained by premiums and performance; poor returns plus low premiums can cause lapse. Also a security.
PolicyPremiumCash valueDeath benefitSecurity?
TermLow, fixed for termNoneFixed (or decreasing)No
WholeFixedGuaranteedGuaranteedNo
UniversalFlexibleCurrent rate, minimum guaranteedAdjustableNo
VariableFixedNot guaranteedGuaranteed minimumYes
Variable universalFlexibleNot guaranteedNot guaranteedYes

Taxation

  • Death benefits are generally received income-tax-free by beneficiaries. If the insured owns the policy, the death benefit is included in the insured's gross estate for estate tax purposes (one reason for an irrevocable life insurance trust).
  • Cash value grows tax-deferred. For a standard policy, withdrawals are taxed FIFO — basis (premiums paid) comes out first tax-free. Policy loans are not taxable while the policy stays in force.
  • A modified endowment contract (MEC) — a policy funded too quickly under the IRS 7-pay test — loses the favorable treatment: distributions and loans are taxed LIFO (gains first) and are subject to a 10% penalty before 59½, much like a non-qualified annuity. The death benefit remains income-tax-free.
  • Surrendering a policy for more than total premiums paid produces ordinary income on the gain.
Exam tip: "Maximum coverage for the lowest cost" → term. "Premium flexibility and investment control" → variable universal life. "Guaranteed minimum death benefit with investment-linked cash value and fixed premium" → variable life.
Trap: In variable life, the death benefit has a guaranteed minimum, but the cash value does not. Don't reverse them.
keyPoints: Term: temporary pure protection, no cash value, most coverage per premium dollar.
Whole life: fixed premium, guaranteed cash value and death benefit; insurer bears investment risk.
Universal life: flexible premium and death benefit; cash value earns current rate with minimum guarantee.
Variable life: fixed premium, separate account, cash value not guaranteed, minimum death benefit guaranteed; a security.
Variable universal life: flexible premiums plus separate account; nothing guaranteed; a security.
Death benefits are generally income-tax-free to beneficiaries but included in the insured's estate if the insured owned the policy.
Non-MEC withdrawals are FIFO (basis first); MEC distributions are LIFO with a 10% penalty before 59½.
