topics.title: Other Assets: Commodities, Precious Metals and Digital Assets
topics.reading:
Commodities

Commodities are raw materials — energy (crude oil, natural gas), metals (gold, copper), and agricultural products (wheat, corn, cattle). Investors gain exposure through futures contracts, commodity pools and managed futures funds, commodity ETFs/ETNs, or stocks of commodity producers.

  • Benefits: potential inflation hedge (commodity prices often rise with inflation) and diversification because commodity returns have historically had low correlation with stocks and bonds.
  • Risks: high volatility; prices driven by weather, geopolitics, supply disruptions and currency moves; leverage in futures; no income (no dividends or interest).
  • Futures-based funds face roll costs: when later contracts are priced above near-term contracts (contango), rolling positions can cause the fund to lag the spot price over time.
  • Commodity futures and pools are regulated by the CFTC, with NFA oversight.

Precious metals

Gold, silver and platinum are held as physical bullion and coins, through ETFs backed by physical metal, futures, or mining stocks.

  • Viewed as a store of value and hedge against inflation, currency debasement and crisis (gold often rises when confidence falls).
  • Drawbacks: no income, storage and insurance costs for physical metal, dealer markups, and significant price volatility.
  • Tax: physical precious metals are collectibles; long-term gains are taxed at a maximum federal rate of 28% rather than the lower long-term capital gains rates. ETFs structured as grantor trusts that hold physical metal generally receive the same collectibles treatment.
  • Mining stocks provide leveraged, company-specific exposure: they carry business, management and operating risk in addition to metal price risk.

Digital assets

Digital assets include cryptocurrencies (bitcoin, ether), stablecoins and tokens recorded on a blockchain — a decentralized, distributed ledger. Exposure can come from direct ownership, exchange-traded products (spot bitcoin and ether ETPs began trading in 2024), futures, or companies in the industry.

  • Volatility: prices can swing dramatically in days; drawdowns of 50%+ have happened repeatedly. Crypto produces no cash flows, making valuation speculative.
  • Custody: ownership is controlled by private keys. Lost keys mean lost assets; stolen keys mean theft with little recourse. "Hot" wallets (online) are convenient but more exposed to hacking; "cold" storage (offline) is more secure. Assets left on a trading platform are exposed to that platform's failure. Advisers with custody must consider whether a qualified custodian can properly hold the asset.
  • Regulatory uncertainty: whether a given token is a security (SEC), a commodity (CFTC) or something else has been contested and the framework is still evolving; state regulators and NASAA have issued investor alerts about crypto fraud and unregistered offerings.
  • Other risks: fraud and manipulation, platform insolvency, lack of SIPC protection for most crypto holdings, liquidity crunches, and operational/technology risk.
  • Tax: the IRS treats virtual currency as property. Selling, exchanging or spending it is a taxable event producing capital gain or loss.

Suitability

Commodities, metals and crypto are generally considered satellite positions: a modest allocation for diversification or inflation protection, appropriate only for clients who can tolerate high volatility and who do not need current income. An adviser should disclose the unique risks and ensure the position size fits the client's objectives and risk tolerance.

Exam tip: Commodities and precious metals = inflation hedge and low correlation, but no income. Crypto questions focus on volatility, custody (private keys) and regulatory uncertainty.
Trap: Gains on physical gold held over a year are not taxed at the 15%/20% long-term rates — collectibles face a 28% maximum rate. And crypto is property for tax purposes, not currency.
keyPoints: Commodities offer an inflation hedge and low correlation with stocks and bonds, but are volatile and pay no income.
Futures-based commodity funds face roll costs (contango) and can lag spot prices.
Physical precious metals have storage and insurance costs; long-term gains are taxed as collectibles at up to 28%.
Mining stocks add company-specific business risk to metal price risk.
Crypto risks: extreme volatility, custody and private-key risk, platform failure, fraud, and evolving regulation.
The IRS treats virtual currency as property: selling, exchanging or spending it is a taxable event.
Alternatives such as metals and crypto are generally small satellite positions for clients who can tolerate volatility.

It is a common way for municipalities to fund construction projects
It usually pays semiannual interest coupons
questions.explanation: Commercial paper is unsecured short-term corporate debt with a maximum maturity of 270 days, which exempts it from SEC registration. It is generally issued at a discount, not with coupons, and it is a corporate (not municipal) instrument. The choice about receivables is wrong because commercial paper is unsecured.

questions.q:
Which of the following would be considered money market instruments?
I. Treasury bills
II. Bankers' acceptances
III. Negotiable jumbo CDs
IV. 10-year Treasury notes with 8 years remaining to maturity
questions.explanation: Money market instruments are short-term debt with one year or less to maturity: T-bills, bankers' acceptances, negotiable CDs, commercial paper and repos. A Treasury note with 8 years remaining is intermediate-term debt, not a money market instrument, regardless of the issuer's safety.

questions.q: A client wants to keep an emergency reserve equal to six months of expenses. The investment adviser representative recommends a money market mutual fund. Which risk remains most significant for this holding over time?
questions.explanation: Cash equivalents are liquid, have minimal price sensitivity to interest rates and minimal default risk, but their low returns may not keep pace with inflation. Interest rate risk is minimal because the underlying instruments mature within days or months.

questions.q: An importer of goods needs short-term financing that is guaranteed by its bank so that the foreign exporter will accept payment at a future date. The instrument most likely used is
questions.explanation: A bankers' acceptance is a time draft that a bank accepts (guarantees), used specifically to finance international trade. Commercial paper is an unsecured corporate note not tied to a specific trade transaction; a negotiable CD is a bank deposit; a repo is a collateralized short-term loan between dealers or institutions.

questions.q: A client in a high-tax state wants to minimize state income tax on her bond interest while avoiding default risk. Which investment best meets her objective?
questions.explanation: Treasury interest is exempt from state and local income tax, and Treasuries carry full faith and credit backing. GNMA certificates are also backed by full faith and credit, but their interest is taxable at the federal, state and local levels, making GNMA the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) are TRUE?
I. The principal is adjusted based on changes in the CPI.
II. The coupon rate is adjusted based on changes in the CPI.
III. The annual inflation adjustment to principal is taxable in the year it occurs.
IV. TIPS generally have a higher coupon rate than a conventional Treasury of the same maturity.
questions.explanation: TIPS adjust principal, not the coupon rate, for inflation. The fixed rate is applied to the adjusted principal, so the dollar interest rises with inflation. The annual adjustment is taxed as phantom income. Because inflation protection is built in, TIPS normally have a lower stated coupon than a comparable conventional Treasury.

questions.q: Parents want to fund a known college tuition bill due in 15 years and do not want to worry about reinvesting interest payments. Which investment best eliminates reinvestment risk?
questions.explanation: Zero-coupon securities such as STRIPS pay no periodic interest, so there is nothing to reinvest; the return is locked in if held to maturity. Treasury bonds and GNMAs make periodic payments that must be reinvested at future rates, and GNMAs also return principal early.

questions.q: Which of the following mortgage-related securities is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government?
questions.explanation: GNMA is a government-owned corporation and its pass-through certificates carry an explicit full faith and credit guarantee. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are government-sponsored enterprises with only implied backing; private-label CMOs have no government guarantee.

questions.q: Interest rates drop sharply. An investor holding mortgage-backed pass-through securities is most likely to experience
choices: a reduction in monthly principal payments
a sharp increase in the securities' price with no ceiling
questions.explanation: Falling rates prompt homeowners to refinance, so principal is returned early and must be reinvested at lower rates — prepayment risk. This also limits price appreciation (negative convexity). Extension risk occurs when rates rise and prepayments slow.

questions.q: Within a collateralized mortgage obligation, which tranche offers the most predictable cash flows?
questions.explanation: PAC tranches receive principal on a set schedule because companion tranches absorb prepayment and extension variability. Companion tranches are therefore the most volatile. Z-tranches accrue interest and receive nothing until earlier tranches are retired, which makes their timing less certain.

questions.q: All of the following are true of GNMA pass-through certificates EXCEPT
choices: each payment includes both interest and principal
interest is exempt from state income tax
they are subject to prepayment risk
questions.explanation: GNMA interest is taxable at the federal, state and local levels; the state-tax exemption applies to direct Treasury obligations, not GNMAs. GNMA pass-throughs do pay monthly, include principal and interest, and carry prepayment risk.

questions.q: A bond backed by a pool of automobile loans is best described as
questions.explanation: Asset-backed securities are backed by non-mortgage receivables such as auto loans, credit card balances and student loans. An equipment trust certificate is secured by equipment the issuer owns (like aircraft); a collateral trust bond is secured by securities the issuer owns.

questions.q:
A corporation is liquidated. In what order are the following paid?
I. Common stockholders
II. Secured bondholders
III. Preferred stockholders
IV. Debenture holders
questions.explanation: Secured creditors come first (to the extent of their collateral), then unsecured creditors such as debenture holders, then preferred stockholders, and common stockholders last. Placing preferred ahead of debentures is the common error — preferred is equity, and all debt ranks ahead of equity.

questions.q: An airline issues bonds secured by its fleet of aircraft. These bonds are
questions.explanation: Equipment trust certificates are secured by rolling stock or other equipment, such as airplanes and rail cars, and are typical of transportation companies. Mortgage bonds are secured by real property; collateral trust bonds by securities; debentures are unsecured.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding general obligation (GO) municipal bonds is TRUE?
choices: They are backed by the revenues of a specific facility
They are backed by the full faith, credit and taxing power of the issuer
They are analyzed primarily through a feasibility study
They do not require voter approval
questions.explanation: GO bonds are backed by the issuer's taxing power and generally require voter approval. Revenue bonds are backed by a facility's revenues and analyzed with a feasibility study, and they typically do not need voter approval.

questions.q: A resident of New Jersey purchases a municipal bond issued by the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. The interest is
choices: exempt from federal income tax only
taxable at the federal level but exempt from New Jersey tax
taxable at both the federal and state level
exempt from both federal and New Jersey income tax
questions.explanation: Bonds issued by U.S. territories such as Puerto Rico, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands are exempt from federal income tax and from income tax in every state. An out-of-state municipal bond from another state would normally be taxable by New Jersey, which makes 'federal only' the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: An investor buys a municipal general obligation bond at par ($1,000) and sells it two years later for $1,060. Which statement is correct regarding taxation?
choices: The interest received and the gain are both tax-exempt
The interest is federally tax-exempt, but the gain is subject to capital gains tax
The interest is taxable, but the gain is tax-exempt
The entire $60 is treated as tax-exempt interest
questions.explanation: Municipal bond interest is generally exempt from federal income tax, but the $60 gain on sale ($1,060 − $1,000) is a taxable capital gain. The tax exemption applies only to the interest, never to profits from selling the bond.

questions.q: A U.S. investor wants to buy bonds of a German corporation but does not want exposure to currency risk. Which of the following would be most appropriate?
choices: A Eurodollar bond issued by the German corporation
A euro-denominated bond issued by the German corporation
questions.explanation: Eurodollar bonds are denominated in U.S. dollars, so a U.S. investor receives interest and principal in dollars with no exchange-rate exposure. A euro-denominated bond has currency risk. An ADR is equity, and although it trades in dollars, it still reflects currency movements in the underlying shares.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about Yankee bonds are TRUE?
I. They are issued by foreign issuers.
II. They are denominated in U.S. dollars.
III. They are issued outside the United States.
IV. They are registered with the SEC.
questions.explanation: Yankee bonds are dollar-denominated bonds issued in the United States by foreign issuers and registered with the SEC. Bonds issued outside the U.S. in dollars are Eurodollar bonds, so statement III is false.

questions.q: Compared with a nonconvertible bond of the same issuer, quality and maturity, a convertible bond will typically have
questions.explanation: Investors accept a lower coupon on a convertible bond in exchange for the potential to share in the appreciation of the common stock. The conversion feature does not change the bond's credit rating or its place in the capital structure.

questions.q: A 6% corporate bond is trading at 120. What is its current yield?
questions.explanation: A price of 120 means 120% of $1,000 par, or $1,200. Annual interest is 6% of par = $60. Current yield = $60 ÷ $1,200 = 5.0%. The 7.2% answer comes from multiplying 6% by 1.2 instead of dividing.

questions.q: A bond with a 5% coupon is callable at par in five years and matures in 20 years. It is currently trading at a discount. Which yield is highest?
questions.explanation: For a discount bond: nominal < current yield < YTM < YTC. If the bond is called early, the discount (the gain back to par) is earned over fewer years, so YTC is highest. The nominal yield is the lowest.

questions.q: An investor buys a bond at a premium. Which of the following correctly ranks its yields from highest to lowest?
questions.explanation: For a premium bond: nominal > current yield > YTM > YTC. The premium lowers current yield below the coupon rate, the loss of the premium at maturity pulls YTM lower, and an early call forces that loss over fewer years, making YTC lowest. The ranking that starts with YTC as the highest is the discount-bond order, the reverse of the premium order.

questions.q: An investor in the 35% federal tax bracket is considering a municipal bond yielding 3.9%. What is the tax-equivalent yield?
questions.explanation: Tax-equivalent yield = municipal yield ÷ (1 − tax rate) = 3.9% ÷ 0.65 = 6.00%. 5.27% results from multiplying by 1.35, a common error. 2.54% is the muni yield multiplied by 0.65, which is the formula for converting a taxable yield to after-tax, applied to the wrong bond.

questions.q: A client in the 24% federal bracket (no state income tax) is choosing between a 5.0% corporate bond and a 3.9% municipal bond of similar quality and maturity. Which statement is correct?
choices: The corporate bond provides the higher after-tax yield, 3.8%
The municipal bond provides the higher after-tax yield
The two provide equal after-tax yields
The corporate bond's after-tax yield is 4.4%
questions.explanation: After-tax corporate yield = 5.0% × (1 − 0.24) = 3.8%, which is less than the 3.9% muni. Equivalently, the muni's tax-equivalent yield is 3.9 ÷ 0.76 = 5.13%, above 5.0%. So the muni wins, though narrowly. The first choice has the right after-tax number but the wrong conclusion.

questions.q: Which of the following bonds would experience the greatest percentage price change if interest rates rise by 1%?
questions.explanation: Duration — price sensitivity — increases with longer maturity and lower coupon. A zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, so the 20-year zero has a duration of 20, higher than the 20-year 8% bond, whose coupons shorten its duration.

questions.q: A bond portfolio has a duration of 7 years. If market interest rates increase by 0.5%, the portfolio's value will change by approximately
questions.explanation: Approximate price change = −duration × change in yield = −7 × 0.5% = −3.5%. Prices fall when rates rise, so a positive change is wrong; −7% would correspond to a full 1% rate rise.

questions.q: Which of the following ratings is the lowest that would still be considered investment grade?
questions.explanation: Investment grade is BBB-/Baa3 or higher. Baa3 is the lowest Moody's investment-grade rating. BB+ (S&P) and Ba1 (Moody's) are the highest speculative-grade ratings, just one notch below investment grade — a classic trap.

questions.q: All of the following statements about call features on bonds are true EXCEPT
choices: issuers are most likely to call bonds when interest rates have fallen
callable bonds generally offer higher yields than comparable noncallable bonds
a call feature primarily benefits the bondholder
questions.explanation: A call feature benefits the issuer, which can refinance when rates drop, leaving the investor with reinvestment risk and capped price appreciation. That is why callable bonds must offer higher yields. It is the put feature that benefits the bondholder.

questions.q: During the early stages of a recession, the yield spread between high-yield corporate bonds and Treasury securities will most likely
choices: narrow, as investors seek higher returns
widen, as investors move to higher-quality securities
remain unchanged, since both are affected equally by interest rates
questions.explanation: In a weakening economy, default risk rises and investors sell lower-quality bonds and buy Treasuries (a flight to quality). High-yield prices fall and their yields rise relative to Treasuries, so the credit spread widens. Spreads narrow during expansions.

questions.q: A $1,000 par convertible bond is convertible into common stock at $40 per share. The bond is trading at $1,100. What is the parity price of the common stock?
questions.explanation: Conversion ratio = $1,000 ÷ $40 = 25 shares. Parity price of the stock = bond's market price ÷ conversion ratio = $1,100 ÷ 25 = $44. $40 is the conversion price (fixed at issue), not parity; $25 is the conversion ratio.

questions.q: A $100 par preferred stock is convertible into common at $25. The common stock is trading at $28. At what price would the preferred stock be at parity?
questions.explanation: Conversion ratio = $100 ÷ $25 = 4 shares. Parity price of the preferred = stock price × conversion ratio = $28 × 4 = $112. If the preferred traded below $112, converting and selling the stock would be profitable.

questions.q: A $1,000 convertible bond has a conversion price of $50 and is trading at $980. The common stock is trading at $52. Which of the following is TRUE?
choices: The bond is trading at parity
The bond is trading at a premium to its conversion value
An arbitrage opportunity exists by buying the bond and converting
Conversion would result in a loss compared with selling the bond
questions.explanation: Conversion ratio = 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20. Conversion value = 20 × $52 = $1,040, which exceeds the $980 bond price. Buying the bond for $980, converting to 20 shares and selling them for $1,040 captures a $60 profit before costs — an arbitrage opportunity. The bond is at a discount to, not a premium to, conversion value.

questions.q: A company has 6%, $100 par cumulative preferred stock outstanding. It paid no preferred dividends last year and paid only $2 per share the year before. This year, before any common dividend can be paid, preferred holders must receive
questions.explanation: Arrears: $4 unpaid from two years ago ($6 − $2) plus $6 from last year = $10, plus the current year's $6 = $16 per share. $18 assumes nothing at all was paid two years ago.

questions.q: A U.S. investor buys an ADR of a Japanese company. Which of the following statements is TRUE?
choices: Because ADRs trade in dollars, the investor has no currency risk
Dividends are paid in yen directly to the investor
The ADR is issued by the Japanese company to U.S. investors
A strengthening dollar relative to the yen would tend to reduce the ADR's value
questions.explanation: The ADR's value reflects the yen price of the underlying shares converted to dollars. If the dollar strengthens, each yen is worth fewer dollars, so the ADR tends to fall. ADRs trade in dollars and dividends are converted to dollars by the U.S. depositary bank — which issues the ADR — but currency risk remains.

questions.q: Which type of preferred stock would most likely pay the highest stated dividend rate, all else being equal?
questions.explanation: A call feature benefits the issuer, who can redeem the stock when rates fall, so investors demand a higher dividend. Convertible, cumulative and participating features each give the holder an advantage, so those issues can pay lower stated rates.

questions.q: An investor owns 300 shares of XYZ. Five directors are up for election, and XYZ uses cumulative voting. Which of the following is TRUE?
choices: The investor may cast a maximum of 300 votes for any one candidate
The investor may cast 1,500 votes in any combination, including all for one candidate
The investor has 300 votes in total to split among the candidates
The investor may cast 1,500 votes but no more than 300 for one candidate
questions.explanation: Under cumulative voting, total votes = shares × seats = 300 × 5 = 1,500, which may be distributed in any manner, including all 1,500 for a single candidate. The limit of 300 per candidate describes statutory voting.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about rights and warrants are TRUE?
I. Rights typically allow purchase at a price below the current market price.
II. Warrants typically have an exercise price above the market price when issued.
III. Rights are generally long-term instruments.
IV. Warrants are often issued as a sweetener with bonds.
questions.explanation: Rights are short-term (typically 30-45 days) with a subscription price below market. Warrants are long-term with an exercise price above market at issuance and are often attached to bonds or preferred stock to make them more attractive. Statement III is false.

questions.q: The main purpose of a preemptive right is to
choices: allow shareholders to maintain their proportionate ownership
give shareholders the right to vote on the dividend
allow the company to buy back shares at a discount
provide a long-term option to buy shares above market price
questions.explanation: Preemptive rights let existing shareholders buy newly issued shares before the public, so they can maintain their percentage of ownership and avoid dilution. Shareholders do not vote on dividends; a long-term option priced above market describes a warrant.

questions.q: Under the current T+1 regular-way settlement cycle, a company declares a dividend with a record date of Thursday, the 15th. What is the last day an investor can buy the stock in a regular-way trade and still receive the dividend?
questions.explanation: With T+1 settlement, the ex-dividend date is the record date (Thursday). A buyer must purchase before the ex-date, so the last day to buy with the dividend is Wednesday, the 14th, which settles on Thursday, the record date. A Thursday purchase settles Friday, after the record date.

questions.q: An officer of a publicly traded, SEC-reporting company wants to sell shares of company stock she bought in the open market three years ago. Under Rule 144, which of the following applies?
choices: She may not sell because she is an insider
She must hold the shares one more year
She is subject to the volume limitations of Rule 144
The shares are restricted securities because she is an officer
questions.explanation: As an officer, she is an affiliate, so her shares are control stock even though they were bought in the open market. Control stock has no holding period (that applies to restricted stock), but the sale is subject to Rule 144's volume limits — the greater of 1% of outstanding shares or the average weekly trading volume over the prior four weeks in any 90-day period. Her shares are not restricted, because they were not acquired in an unregistered transaction.

questions.q: An employee exercises non-qualified stock options (NSOs) to buy 1,000 shares at $20 when the stock is trading at $35. What are the tax consequences at exercise?
choices: No tax is due until the shares are sold
$15,000 is an AMT preference item only
questions.explanation: For NSOs, the spread at exercise ($35 − $20 = $15 × 1,000 = $15,000) is ordinary compensation income, and the cost basis becomes $35 per share. The AMT-preference treatment describes ISOs, not NSOs — the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: An employee holding incentive stock options (ISOs) wants the entire gain on her shares taxed as long-term capital gain. Which holding requirement must she meet?
choices: Hold the shares more than one year from the grant date
Hold the shares more than two years from the grant date and more than one year from the exercise date
Hold the shares more than one year from the grant date and more than two years from the exercise date
Hold the options for at least three years before exercising
questions.explanation: For a qualifying disposition of ISO stock, shares must be held more than two years from grant and more than one year from exercise. If she sells sooner (a disqualifying disposition), the spread at exercise is taxed as ordinary income.

questions.q: ABC Corp. just paid an annual dividend of $2.00. Dividends are expected to grow at 5% per year, and investors require a 9% return. Using the constant-growth dividend discount model, what is the stock's value?
questions.explanation: First find next year's dividend: D1 = $2.00 × 1.05 = $2.10. Value = D1 ÷ (r − g) = $2.10 ÷ (0.09 − 0.05) = $52.50. $50.00 incorrectly uses the dividend just paid (D0) instead of D1; $22.22 divides by the required return alone.

questions.q: A straight (nonconvertible) preferred stock pays a $6 annual dividend. If an investor requires an 8% return, what is the most the investor should pay for the stock?
questions.explanation: Straight preferred stock is a perpetuity, valued with the zero-growth dividend discount model: value = D ÷ r = $6 ÷ 0.08 = $75. $100 is a common par value, not the value at the required return.

questions.q: A research analyst reviewing a stock notes its 200-day moving average, trading volume, and a recent breakout above a resistance level. This analyst is using
questions.explanation: Technical analysis studies price and volume data — moving averages, support and resistance, chart patterns — to time purchases and sales. Fundamental analysis studies financial statements, management, the industry and the economy to estimate intrinsic value.

questions.q:
Which of the following would be used by a fundamental analyst?
I. The company's debt-to-equity ratio
II. Head-and-shoulders patterns
III. The company's price-to-earnings ratio
IV. The advance/decline line
questions.explanation: Fundamental analysts use financial statement data and valuation ratios such as debt-to-equity and P/E. Chart patterns like head-and-shoulders and market breadth measures like the advance/decline line are technical tools.

questions.q: An investment requires $10,000 today and is expected to return $11,000 in one year. If the investor's required rate of return is 12%, which statement is correct?
choices: The net present value is positive, so the investment should be accepted
The internal rate of return is 12%
The net present value is negative, so the investment should be rejected
The present value of the cash flow is $11,000
questions.explanation: PV = $11,000 ÷ 1.12 = $9,821. NPV = $9,821 − $10,000 = −$179. A negative NPV means the investment returns less than the 12% required — its IRR is 10% ($1,000 ÷ $10,000) — so it should be rejected.

questions.q: A technical analyst notices that short interest in a stock has risen to a very high level. The analyst would most likely interpret this as
choices: bearish, because many investors expect the stock to fall
neutral, because short interest does not affect price
bearish, because it signals that insiders are selling
bullish, because short sellers must eventually buy shares to cover their positions
questions.explanation: High short interest is considered a bullish, contrarian indicator: every short position represents future buying demand when it is covered. Although short sellers are betting on a decline, the technical interpretation focuses on the latent demand.

questions.q:
Under the constant-growth dividend discount model, which of the following changes would increase a stock's value, all else equal?
I. An increase in the expected dividend growth rate
II. An increase in the investor's required rate of return
III. A decrease in interest rates that lowers the required rate of return
IV. A decrease in next year's expected dividend
questions.explanation: Value = D1 ÷ (r − g). A higher g shrinks the denominator, raising value; a lower r also shrinks the denominator, raising value. A higher required return or a lower expected dividend reduces value.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a secondary distribution?
choices: The issuer sells newly authorized shares to the public for the first time
The issuer sells additional new shares after its IPO
Large existing shareholders sell their shares to the public, with the proceeds going to them
The issuer sells shares to existing shareholders through a rights offering
questions.explanation: In a secondary distribution, existing holders sell shares they already own, and the proceeds go to them — not the company — so there is no dilution. The first choice describes an IPO and the second a follow-on primary offering; both put money in the issuer's hands.

questions.q: During the cooling-off period for an initial public offering, a registered representative may
choices: accept indications of interest and deliver a preliminary prospectus
accept customer orders subject to the final price
tell customers the SEC has approved the offering
send customers a final prospectus with the offering price
questions.explanation: During the cooling-off period (at least 20 days after filing), no sales or binding orders are allowed, but indications of interest may be taken and the preliminary prospectus (red herring) may be distributed. The SEC never approves securities, and the final prospectus with the price is available only at effectiveness.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements about special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs) are TRUE?
I. At the time of the IPO, the SPAC has no operating business.
II. IPO proceeds are generally held in a trust account until an acquisition is completed.
III. Shareholders generally may redeem their shares for a pro rata portion of the trust when a merger is proposed.
IV. The trust account guarantees that the post-merger stock will trade at or above the IPO price.
questions.explanation: SPACs are blank check companies with no operations at IPO; proceeds are held in trust; and shareholders can typically redeem their shares at the merger vote. The trust protects the cash only until the de-SPAC — it provides no guarantee about the post-merger trading price, which often falls below the IPO price.

questions.q: A client asks what a 'blind pool' offering is. The best explanation is an offering in which
choices: the identity of the underwriter is not disclosed to investors
the specific properties or businesses to be acquired are not identified when investors commit funds
the offering price is not set until after the sale
investors' identities are kept confidential from the issuer
questions.explanation: In a blind pool, investors commit money before the sponsor identifies the specific assets or businesses to be acquired, so they rely entirely on the sponsor's judgment. This makes blind pools riskier than offerings with specified assets.

questions.q: In a firm commitment underwriting of an IPO, which party bears the risk of unsold shares?
questions.explanation: In a firm commitment, the underwriter buys the entire issue from the issuer and resells it, so the underwriter bears the risk of any unsold shares. In a best efforts underwriting, the underwriter acts only as an agent and unsold shares remain with the issuer.

questions.q: Which of the following characteristics applies to a closed-end management company but NOT to an open-end management company?
choices: Shares may trade at a premium or discount to net asset value
Shares are redeemable by the fund at net asset value
The fund continuously offers new shares to the public
Purchases are made at the next computed net asset value plus any sales charge
questions.explanation: Closed-end fund shares trade in the secondary market, so their price is set by supply and demand and can be above or below NAV. Redeemability, continuous offering and forward pricing at NAV plus a load are all features of open-end (mutual) funds.

questions.q: An investment company that holds a fixed portfolio of municipal bonds, has no board of directors, does not employ an investment adviser, and will terminate when the bonds mature is BEST described as
questions.explanation: A UIT holds a fixed, supervised (not managed) portfolio, has no board of directors or investment adviser, and terminates on a stated date. A closed-end fund is a management company with a board and an adviser, even though its share count is fixed.

questions.q: A client wants to buy a broad stock index fund but insists on being able to use a limit order and to sell during the trading day if the market drops sharply. The MOST appropriate vehicle is
choices: an index unit investment trust purchased from the sponsor
Class A shares of an index mutual fund
questions.explanation: ETFs trade on exchanges throughout the day at market prices, so investors can use limit and stop orders and exit intraday. Mutual fund orders — no-load or loaded — are all filled at the next computed NAV after the order, usually at the close, and limit orders are not possible.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements regarding exchange-traded funds are TRUE?
I. They may be purchased on margin.
II. Retail investors typically redeem shares directly with the fund at NAV.
III. They can be sold short.
IV. Investors buying them pay the bid-ask spread.
questions.explanation: ETFs trade like stocks: they can be bought on margin, sold short, and investors pay the bid-ask spread. Retail investors do not redeem with the fund; only authorized participants create and redeem creation units, so statement II is false.

questions.q: All of the following are types of investment companies under the Investment Company Act of 1940 EXCEPT
questions.explanation: The three classes of investment companies are face-amount certificate companies, UITs and management companies (open-end and closed-end). A REIT is a real estate company organized as a corporation or trust and qualifying for special tax treatment — it is not an investment company.

questions.q: To avoid paying corporate income tax on distributed income, a real estate investment trust must distribute at least what percentage of its taxable income to shareholders?
questions.explanation: A REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income (and meet asset and income tests) to receive conduit treatment. The 75% figure is the asset/income test for real estate holdings, not the distribution requirement.

questions.q: A client in a high tax bracket wants real estate exposure that will allow her to deduct depreciation losses against other income. Which statement about a publicly traded REIT is MOST accurate?
choices: A REIT will meet her objective because it is a pass-through entity for both income and losses
A REIT will meet her objective because its dividends are qualified and taxed at lower rates
A REIT will not meet her objective because REITs cannot own depreciable property
A REIT will not meet her objective because losses do not pass through to shareholders
questions.explanation: REITs pass through income, but not losses, to shareholders. Pass-through of losses is a feature of direct participation programs such as limited partnerships. REIT dividends are generally non-qualified, and equity REITs certainly own depreciable property — the depreciation simply stays at the REIT level.

questions.q: Which of the following individuals meets the definition of an accredited investor?
choices: A married investor with a $1.3 million net worth, of which $600,000 is equity in the primary residence
A single investor who earned $230,000 in each of the past two years and expects the same this year
A single investor who earned $250,000 last year after earning $120,000 the year before
A married couple with joint income of $280,000 in each of the past two years
questions.explanation: An individual qualifies with income over $200,000 in each of the two most recent years with a reasonable expectation of the same this year. The $1.3 million net worth falls to $700,000 after excluding the primary residence; the single investor fails the two-year test; and joint income must exceed $300,000.

questions.q: Compared with a publicly traded REIT, a non-traded REIT typically has
choices: less liquidity and higher up-front fees
the ability to pass through operating losses
questions.explanation: Non-traded REITs have no exchange listing, so investors depend on limited, suspendable redemption programs, and they often carry substantial offering costs. Both types must meet the same 90% distribution rule, and neither passes through losses.

questions.q:
Which of the following are typical characteristics of hedge funds?
I. Use of leverage and short selling
II. Performance-based fees
III. Lock-up periods restricting withdrawals
IV. Daily redemption at net asset value
questions.explanation: Hedge funds commonly use leverage, short selling and derivatives, charge a performance fee on top of a management fee, and impose lock-ups and limited redemption windows. Daily redemption at NAV is a mutual fund feature, not a hedge fund feature.

questions.q: A mutual fund has a net asset value of $18.40 and a public offering price of $20.00. What is the sales charge as a percentage of the offering price?
questions.explanation: Sales charge % = (POP − NAV) ÷ POP = ($20.00 − $18.40) ÷ $20.00 = $1.60 ÷ $20.00 = 8.0%. Dividing by NAV instead ($1.60 ÷ $18.40 ≈ 8.7%) is the classic mistake — loads are always stated as a percentage of POP.

questions.q: A fund's Class A shares carry a 5% sales charge and the NAV is $9.50. What is the public offering price?
questions.explanation: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %) = $9.50 ÷ 0.95 = $10.00. Adding 5% to NAV ($9.50 × 1.05 ≈ $9.98) is wrong because the sales charge is a percentage of POP, not NAV.

questions.q: A fund family offers these Class A breakpoints: under $25,000: 5.5%; $25,000–$49,999: 4.75%; $50,000–$99,999: 3.75%. A client invested $20,000 in the family eight months ago under a 13-month letter of intent for $50,000 and now invests $30,000 more. Assuming the letter's terms are met, what sales charge applies to the purchases?
choices: 5.5% on the first $20,000 and 4.75% on the $30,000
5.5% on the first $20,000 and 3.75% on the $30,000
questions.explanation: Under a letter of intent, all purchases covered by the letter receive the breakpoint rate the investor committed to reach, provided the total is invested within 13 months. The client reached $50,000 in month eight, so the entire $50,000 qualifies for 3.75%.

questions.q: A client already holds $42,000 (current value) of Class A shares in a fund family. The family's breakpoint is 4.5% under $50,000 and 3.5% at $50,000 or more. The client buys $10,000 more. Under rights of accumulation, the new purchase will be charged
questions.explanation: Rights of accumulation count existing holdings toward breakpoints on new purchases: $42,000 + $10,000 = $52,000, crossing the $50,000 breakpoint, so the new $10,000 is charged 3.5%. ROA does not refund higher charges paid on earlier purchases.

questions.q: An investor who expects to hold a mutual fund investment for about two years and is investing $15,000 would generally find which share class MOST cost-effective?
choices: Class A with a letter of intent for $50,000
questions.explanation: For short holding periods, Class C's level load (no front-end load and a small first-year CDSC) usually costs less than paying a full front-end load on a $15,000 purchase that won't reach breakpoints. Class B's CDSC would still be high after two years. Signing an LOI the client has no plan to meet would be improper.

questions.q: A client bought shares of a stock mutual fund three months ago. The fund just paid a capital gains distribution, which the client reinvested. How is the distribution taxed?
choices: As a short-term capital gain in the current year
As a long-term capital gain in the current year
It is not taxable because it was reinvested
As ordinary income when the shares are later sold
questions.explanation: Mutual fund capital gains distributions are treated as long-term regardless of how long the shareholder has held the fund, and they are taxable in the year paid even if reinvested. The reinvested amount increases the client's cost basis.

questions.q:
Which of the following are included in a mutual fund's expense ratio?
I. Management (advisory) fees
II. 12b-1 fees
III. Front-end sales charges
IV. Contingent deferred sales charges
questions.explanation: The expense ratio covers ongoing annual operating expenses: management fees, 12b-1 fees and administrative costs. Sales loads (front-end or CDSC) are one-time transaction charges paid by the investor and are not part of the expense ratio.

questions.q:
Which of the following positions are bullish?
I. Long call
II. Short call
III. Long put
IV. Short put
questions.explanation: A long call profits when the stock rises, and a short put profits (keeps the premium) when the stock stays above the strike. Short calls and long puts are bearish positions.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about warrants is TRUE?
choices: They are short-term instruments that expire within 45 days
They are often issued with bonds to make the bonds more attractive
When issued, their exercise price is below the market price of the stock
They are issued by the Options Clearing Corporation
questions.explanation: Warrants are long-term securities issued by the company, often attached to bonds or preferred stock as a sweetener, with an exercise price above market when issued. Short life and a below-market subscription price describe rights.

questions.q: A U.S. importer enters into a private, customized contract with a bank to buy 2 million euros at a set exchange rate in six months. The GREATEST risk unique to this contract, compared with an exchange-traded futures contract, is
questions.explanation: This is a forward contract: customized and traded OTC with no clearinghouse guarantee, so the importer bears the risk that the bank fails to perform. Exchange-traded futures are guaranteed by a clearinghouse and marked to market daily, which minimizes counterparty risk.

questions.q: All of the following are characteristics of futures contracts EXCEPT
choices: the contracts are standardized as to quantity and quality
positions are marked to market daily
the buyer has the right, but not the obligation, to take delivery
questions.explanation: Futures create obligations for both sides — the long must buy and the short must deliver unless the position is closed out. A right without obligation describes an option buyer. Standardization, daily marking to market and exchange trading are all futures features.

questions.q: An investor buys 1 XYZ Oct 45 call at $3. What are the breakeven point and maximum potential loss?
questions.explanation: Call breakeven = strike + premium = $45 + $3 = $48. A call buyer can lose no more than the premium paid: $3 × 100 = $300. Unlimited loss belongs to the uncovered call writer, not the buyer.

questions.q: An investor buys 1 ABC 60 put at $4. At expiration ABC is trading at $51 and the investor closes the position at intrinsic value. What is the result?
questions.explanation: Breakeven = $60 − $4 = $56. At $51, intrinsic value is $9 per share; subtracting the $4 premium leaves a $5 per share gain, or $500 for 100 shares. $900 ignores the premium paid.

questions.q: An investor writes 1 uncovered DEF 70 put for a premium of $5. What is the investor's maximum potential loss?
questions.explanation: The put writer may have to buy stock at $70 that could fall to zero; the $5 premium received offsets part of that. Max loss = (strike − premium) × 100 = ($70 − $5) × 100 = $6,500. Unlimited loss applies to uncovered calls, not puts.

questions.q: A client buys 100 shares of GHI at $52 and simultaneously writes 1 GHI 55 call at $2. What are the client's breakeven and maximum gain?
questions.explanation: In a covered call the premium lowers the breakeven: $52 − $2 = $50. If the stock rises above $55, the shares are called away: gain = ($55 − $52) + $2 = $5 per share = $500. The short call caps the upside, so gain is not unlimited.

questions.q: A client owns 100 shares of JKL purchased at $80. To protect against a decline, she buys 1 JKL 75 put at $3. What is her maximum potential loss?
questions.explanation: Protective put max loss = (stock cost − strike) + premium = ($80 − $75) + $3 = $8 per share, or $800. The put guarantees she can sell at $75, so she loses $5 on the stock plus the $3 premium. Her breakeven is $83.

questions.q: A client has a large, concentrated position in a stock that has appreciated significantly. He wants maximum protection against a price decline while keeping unlimited upside potential. The adviser should recommend
choices: writing covered calls on the stock
questions.explanation: A long put sets a floor at the strike price while leaving upside unlimited (less the premium). Writing covered calls produces income and only limited downside protection — the premium — and caps upside. Buying calls or writing puts adds bullish exposure rather than protection.

questions.q: An investor sold short 100 shares of MNO at $40. Which option position would limit the investor's potential loss?
questions.explanation: A short seller loses when the stock rises, and that loss is theoretically unlimited. Buying a call lets the investor buy the stock at $45 to cover, capping the loss. Writing a put generates income but gives only partial protection equal to the premium; long puts and short calls add bearish exposure.

questions.q: A client invests as a limited partner in an oil and gas limited partnership that generates a $15,000 loss this year. The client's other income consists of a $180,000 salary and $10,000 of dividends, and she has no passive income. How much of the partnership loss can she deduct this year?
questions.explanation: A limited partnership interest is a passive activity, and passive losses may offset only passive income. Salary is earned income and dividends are portfolio income, so neither can absorb the loss. The unused $15,000 is suspended and carried forward until she has passive income or disposes of her entire interest. The $3,000 limit applies to net capital losses, not passive losses.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements regarding limited partnerships are TRUE?
I. The general partner has unlimited liability.
II. Limited partners may participate in day-to-day management without affecting their liability.
III. Income and losses flow through to the partners.
IV. Interests are generally illiquid.
questions.explanation: The GP manages the business and bears unlimited liability; income and losses flow through on a K-1; and there is usually no ready secondary market. A limited partner who takes part in management risks losing limited-liability status, so statement II is false.

questions.q: An investor holds an exchange-traded note linked to a commodity index. The index rises 12% over the year, but the investor suffers a significant loss. The MOST likely cause is
choices: tracking error in the underlying portfolio of futures
a reduction in the note's coupon rate
a change in the fund's net asset value calculation
deterioration of the issuing bank's credit
questions.explanation: An ETN is unsecured debt of the issuer and holds no portfolio, so there is no tracking error in the ETF sense and no NAV-based portfolio. If the issuer's creditworthiness falls or it defaults, the ETN's value can drop even though the index performed well. ETNs typically pay no coupon.

questions.q: A 2x leveraged ETF tracks an index. Over two days, the index rises 10% and then falls 10%. Ignoring fees, the ETF's cumulative return is approximately
questions.explanation: Because the fund resets daily: day 1 +20% ($100 → $120), day 2 −20% ($120 → $96), a 4% loss. The index lost only 1% (100 → 110 → 99), and twice that (−2%) is not what the fund delivers. This compounding effect is why these funds are unsuitable for most long-term investors.

questions.q: An investor buys a principal-protected note issued by a large bank that promises return of principal at maturity plus 80% of any gain in the S&P 500, capped at 30%. Which risk remains even if the note is held to maturity?
choices: The credit risk of the issuing bank
The risk that the S&P 500 falls below its starting level
Interest rate risk on the final payment
The risk that the participation rate is reduced after purchase
questions.explanation: Principal protection is a promise of the issuer; if the bank defaults, the protection fails. A decline in the index is exactly what the protection covers when held to maturity, and the participation rate and cap are fixed at issuance.

questions.q: A 50-year-old client invested $100,000 in a non-qualified deferred annuity that is now worth $160,000. She withdraws $70,000. How will the withdrawal be taxed?
choices: $70,000 is a tax-free return of basis
$60,000 is a long-term capital gain; $10,000 is a tax-free return of basis
$60,000 is ordinary income subject to a 10% penalty; $10,000 is a tax-free return of basis
$70,000 is ordinary income, but no penalty applies because the contract is non-qualified
questions.explanation: Non-annuitized withdrawals are taxed LIFO: the $60,000 of earnings comes out first and is ordinary income, and because she is under 59½ the 10% penalty applies to that taxable amount. The remaining $10,000 is return of her after-tax basis. Annuity gains are never capital gains.

questions.q: A variable annuity has an assumed interest rate (AIR) of 4%. Last month the separate account earned the equivalent of a 3% annual return. Compared with the prior payment, the annuitant's next payment will
questions.explanation: Payments change based on actual return versus the AIR. A 3% return is below the 4% AIR, so the annuity unit value falls and the payment decreases, even though the account earned a positive return.

questions.q:
Which of the following Section 1035 exchanges would be tax-free?
I. A variable annuity for a fixed annuity
II. A whole life policy for a variable annuity
III. A fixed annuity for a universal life policy
IV. A universal life policy for a variable life policy
questions.explanation: Section 1035 allows annuity-to-annuity, life-to-annuity and life-to-life exchanges. An annuity cannot be exchanged tax-free for life insurance, so statement III is not permitted.

questions.q: A retiree wants the largest possible monthly payment from his annuity and has no beneficiaries he wishes to provide for. Which payout option should he select?
questions.explanation: Straight life pays only for the annuitant's lifetime with no guarantees to anyone else, so the insurer can pay the highest monthly amount. Options that promise payments to a beneficiary or a second life lower the monthly payment.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements regarding a variable annuity are TRUE?
I. Assets are held in a separate account.
II. The insurance company bears the investment risk.
III. It is a security, and a prospectus must be delivered.
IV. Payments purchase accumulation units during the accumulation phase.
questions.explanation: In a variable annuity the contract owner, not the insurer, bears investment risk — that is why it is a security requiring a prospectus. Contributions buy accumulation units in the separate account. Insurer-borne investment risk describes a fixed annuity.

questions.q: An equity-indexed annuity differs from a variable annuity in that the equity-indexed annuity
choices: invests premiums directly in the subaccounts chosen by the owner
gives the owner unlimited participation in index gains
provides a minimum guaranteed return while crediting a portion of index gains subject to a cap
questions.explanation: Equity-indexed annuities credit interest based on an index using a participation rate and often a cap, while guaranteeing a minimum return; assets stay in the insurer's general account. Owner-selected subaccounts describe variable annuities. Indexed annuities commonly carry long surrender periods.

questions.q: A 35-year-old investor who expects to need his money for a home down payment in four years asks about purchasing a non-qualified variable annuity for its tax deferral. The adviser's BEST response is that
choices: it is suitable because earnings grow tax-deferred
it is unsuitable because withdrawals would likely face surrender charges and a 10% tax penalty
it is suitable because withdrawals are taxed as return of basis first
it is suitable because the death benefit protects his principal
questions.explanation: Variable annuities are long-term vehicles. A withdrawal in four years would likely incur surrender charges, and earnings withdrawn before 59½ are taxed as ordinary income (LIFO) plus a 10% penalty. Non-qualified withdrawals are earnings first, not basis first.

questions.q: A 30-year-old parent with a tight budget wants the maximum amount of death protection for the next 20 years. The MOST suitable policy is
questions.explanation: Term insurance provides pure protection with no cash value, so it offers the most death benefit per premium dollar. Permanent policies — whole, variable and VUL — build cash value and cost far more for the same face amount.

questions.q: Which type of life insurance offers flexible premiums and allows the policyowner to direct the cash value among investment subaccounts?
questions.explanation: VUL combines universal life's flexible premiums and adjustable death benefit with variable life's separate-account investing. Variable life has a fixed premium; universal life credits a declared interest rate instead of subaccount returns.

questions.q: Regarding a variable life insurance policy, which of the following is guaranteed?
choices: A minimum rate of return on the separate account
The ability to vary premium payments
questions.explanation: Variable life guarantees a minimum death benefit (the initial face amount) as long as premiums are paid. The cash value is invested in the separate account and is not guaranteed. The premium is fixed — flexible premiums are a feature of universal and variable universal life.

questions.q: A client funded a life insurance policy so quickly that it failed the 7-pay test and became a modified endowment contract. At age 52 she takes a $20,000 distribution when the policy has $30,000 of gain. How is the distribution treated?
choices: It is a tax-free return of premiums paid
It is taxable as a long-term capital gain
It is taxable as ordinary income and subject to a 10% penalty
It is tax-free because it reduces the death benefit
questions.explanation: MEC distributions (including loans) are taxed LIFO — gain first — as ordinary income, with a 10% penalty before 59½. With $30,000 of gain, the entire $20,000 is taxable. Basis-first (FIFO) treatment applies only to non-MEC policies.

questions.q:
Which of the following risks are especially associated with holding cryptocurrency directly?
I. Loss or theft of private keys
II. Regulatory uncertainty
III. High price volatility
IV. Guaranteed protection under SIPC if the trading platform fails
questions.explanation: Crypto owners face custody risk (lost or stolen private keys), an evolving regulatory framework and extreme volatility. Most crypto holdings are not securities covered by SIPC, so a platform failure can leave investors as unsecured creditors — statement IV is false.

questions.q: A client sells gold bullion coins she has held for five years at a large profit. The maximum federal tax rate on the long-term gain is
questions.explanation: Physical precious metals are collectibles, and long-term gains on collectibles are taxed at a maximum 28% rate instead of the 0%/15%/20% long-term capital gains rates. 37% is the top ordinary income rate, which would apply only to short-term gains.

questions.q: A client asks why an adviser suggests a small allocation to commodities. The BEST explanation is that commodities
choices: have lower volatility than investment-grade bonds
may hedge inflation and have historically had low correlation with stocks and bonds
are guaranteed to rise when stock prices fall
questions.explanation: Commodities are used for inflation protection and diversification because their returns have tended to move differently from stocks and bonds. They produce no income, are highly volatile, and there is no guarantee they rise when stocks fall.

questions.q: All of the following are disadvantages of owning physical gold bullion EXCEPT
choices: it has historically served as a store of value during periods of inflation and crisis
it produces no interest or dividend income
it involves storage and insurance costs
dealer markups can make buying and selling expensive
questions.explanation: Gold's role as a store of value in inflationary and crisis periods is the main reason investors hold it — an advantage. Lack of income, storage and insurance costs and dealer spreads are real disadvantages of physical metal.
